This prompt response from Altman reflects just how contentious image use for AI tools is right now, while wider regulation to protect creatives’ IP is yet to be seen. For now, legal experts say for brands wanting to experiment with AI images and video, the onus is on them to establish permissions from creators and properly attribute their use, to avoid individual copyright cases.

The news: California Governor Gavin Newsom signs AI safety law.

Why it matters: It’s the first in-nation law that forces developers at major US-based AI companies to publicly disclose their AI safety and security protocols, and includes whistleblower protections for AI workers, in what analysts are saying could set a benchmark for other states to follow. But it also moves in direct opposition to Trump’s recent AI action plan, which all but deregulates the development of AI at these companies on a national level. As the state that houses much of the Silicon Valley tech companies at the forefront of AI development, California is the closest to their inner workings, but brands operating at a national level will need to watch how other regional governments react, and if this policy influences the ongoing regulation battle at a federal level.

The news: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Checkout.

Why it matters: Instant Checkout removes the friction for ChatGPT users — where they previously searched and discovered products on ChatGPT, before clicking through to make the purchase on a brand’s own site, this new feature omits that final step, shortening the purchase journey. It has big implications for brands’ partnership decisions, advertising strategies, and how they design their websites to appeal to both human customers and LLM “crawlers”. Find out more about what it means for fashion here.

The news: Meta debuts three new AI smart glasses models, but demos fail.

Why it matters: At Meta’s annual Meta Connect conference on 17 September in California, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled the first AI smart glasses with an in-lens display, the Meta Display glasses, designed to replace the wearer’s need to get out their phone. But the live tech demos featured a couple of glitches. A demo of the AI glasses’ ability to interpret cooking ingredients in front of the lenses and give the wearer recipe instructions misinterpreted the selection of raw ingredients as a half-cooked dish, and the glasses failed to pick up a live Whatsapp video call demo between Zuckerberg and Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth.

Bosworth later took to Instagram to explain why the demos went wrong. It wasn’t down to the Wi-Fi, as Zuckerberg suggested onstage, but down to the amount of Meta AI glasses in close proximity during the demo, which caused a flood of traffic to Meta’s live AI server, according to Bosworth. It’s a reminder of just how many pieces of the puzzle are required for this nascent tech to function. At $799 a pop, consumers will expect their buzzy AI glasses to work, so Meta has its work cut out to fix any bugs before they become available for US consumers at the end of the month.

The news: US Federal Trade Commission launches inquiry into AI ‘companions’ used by teens.

Why it matters: Tech companies including OpenAI, Meta and Google are being probed by the US regulator over AI chatbots that provide “companionship”, after a series of high-profile suicides and harm among young people linked to their interactions with the tech. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has ordered the companies to share information about how their AI chatbots develop characters and personas, and how they monetise this kind of engagement. It’s also asking tech firms to disclose what measures they have in place to avoid harm, especially among young people, and how they handle personal data from the conversations.

Given that a primary hesitation among luxury brands in their adoption of AI is the risk of losing consumer trust, the industry should watch the case closely. As user trust in conversations with generative AI grows, analysts say this trust will extend to other online activities like shopping. But as AI regulation becomes increasingly fragmented, more of the onus is on brands to develop their own guardrails. The results of the inquiry should provide key insights for brands that are grappling with developing their own AI ethics, and could inform industry standards in future.

The news: Fraudsters use AI to fake defects on resale platforms.

Why it matters: A disturbing trend has been called out on fashion social media this week — some buyers on resale platforms are using AI image generators to fake defects on received items to get refunds. On resale platforms, trust hangs in the balance between a seller’s description of their garment condition and what the item actually looks like. Although a number of the fake defect attempts called out on social media are amusingly bad, some are more realistic, thanks to recent improvements in AI image generators and their usage becoming more commonplace. When Vogue Business reached out to the main resale platforms, they said this was not yet a business concern — suggesting that this type of fraud is still in its infancy. But in order to retain trust, resale platforms will have to stay on the front foot of this new risk, which could mean investing in an enhanced verification process like videos for buyers making defect claims, which is an added cost for the platforms that could be passed onto users. Vinted told Vogue Business it is “closely monitoring the evolving use of AI among our members to ensure it remains consistent with the platform’s usage guidelines”.

The news: Shein appears to use an AI Luigi Mangione as a T-shirt model.

Why it matters: Shein has opened an internal investigation after the product image for a men’s shirt listing on its website featured a model that resembled Luigi Mangione, the person accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson last year. The online retailer has now taken down the image, and told press in a statement: “The image in question was provided by a third-party vendor and was removed immediately upon discovery.” But the image was online long enough to be shared widely on social media, with speculation surrounding whether it was generated using AI. Mangione has amassed a cult following among some in the US who frame him as a folk hero, in opposition to the US healthcare system. This fuelled a surge of clothing emblazoned with Mangione’s face and name being sold online on retailers like Etsy and Ebay. Connecting the dots, this incident is a stark reminder of the importance of human oversight at brands experimenting with AI for more routine image needs like product listings. And it’s a very stark reminder of how undiscerning the AI image generators themselves are at this point — they crawl the good, the bad and the ugly of the internet to produce their images.

The news: Amazon launches Lens Live instant AI image scanning tool.

Why it matters: Amazon already had a visual search tool, Amazon Lens, which allowed customers to upload images or scan barcodes to discover products. But this new live component brings the retailer more in line with Google Lens and Pinterest Lens — shoppers can now point their phones at things they see before them in the real world, and Amazon’s app will suggest similar or matching products on its platform. The new feature will initially be rolled out to “tens of millions” shoppers in the US, and the company has not said when it will be rolled out to further US customers or into other markets. The live lens feature will also integrate with Amazon’s AI shopping assistant Rufus for more product information. It’s clear that Amazon is investing big in its AI-powered shopping features, and this represents the biggest multimodal search development on a retailer’s own platform thus far. How long until competitors follow suit?

Why it matters: The initial buzz around the launch of ChatGPT-5 and its “PhD-level” knowledge this month has wound down, amid criticisms of the update as somewhat underwhelming. Social media users, tech influencers and journalists abound have commented on the tool’s tendency to “hallucinate” as well as only marginal improvements in its natural language style. One thing that could benefit fashion, however, is OpenAI’s big new emphasis on health — the company wants users to consult ChatGPT like their doctor. But why does this affect fashion brands? Experts tell me that when users are confiding in the tool about their health, and it’s giving them useful recommendations, their trust in the tool will increase exponentially. Trust will likely then extend to other avenues, such as shopping queries and style advice. Let’s see how this plays out in the coming months.

The news: J Crew sparks backlash for unlabelled AI campaign imagery.

Why it matters: This week, newsletter Blackbird Spyplane published a visual investigation of J Crew’s latest campaign — the launch of a collab with Vans — in which the images gave a strong indication they’d been generated by AI. Spyplane managed to uncover the creator of the images — AI photographer Sam Finn. This sparked widespread backlash on social media and within fashion communities, partly because the brand hadn’t credited the use of AI for its images, and partly because, as Spyplane put it, J Crew had “used AI to counterfeit their own vibes”. The images in question resemble J Crew’s catalogue imagery from its late ’80s to early ’90s heyday, which made the use of AI for such an authentic vintage aesthetic even more puzzling to internet critics. The brand has yet to confirm its use of AI, but it did update the campaign instagram post to credit Finn for the “digital art”. (J Crew has not responded to Vogue Business’s request for comment on the campaign.) It’s the latest in a string of AI image controversies across fashion that shows just how thorny the issue is within creative communities. Is there a way that fashion brands can get AI images right?

The news: Meta partners with Midjourney on AI images and video.

Why it matters: Meta made its first move into AI image generation last year, when it launched image generation tool Imagine on its Facebook, Instagram and Messenger platforms. Now, it’s partnering with Midjourney — which is widely viewed as one of the best AI image generation tools on the market — to “bring beauty to billions”, according to chief AI officer Alexandr Wang. It’s the latest move from Meta in its huge AI investment push, and could now enable it to develop image and video products that compete with Google’s Veo and OpenAI’s Sora — and could impact the visual content consumers grow more accustomed to seeing on its social platforms.

The news: Meta is implementing an AI hiring freeze, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal.

Why it matters: After spending the past few months hiring over 50 AI researchers, Meta has hit pause, the tech giant confirmed to The Wall Street Journal. The hiring freeze coincides with a wider restructuring of Meta’s AI teams, which involves splitting them into four divisions. As AI becomes an increasing priority, businesses are not only competing in an AI talent war, but they are having to figure out the internal infrastructures, too. Already, investors are concerned about the stock-based compensation tech giants are offering AI talent, which could dilute shareholder value.

The news: Google adds agentic capabilities to AI Mode search function.

Why it matters: The agentic update allows AI Mode to make restaurant reservations with multiple constraints and preferences (“I only have an hour and need a quick lunch spot, any suggestions?”). The feature will soon expand to local service appointments and event tickets. The update signals a major step towards AI assistants functioning as agents and navigating real-world systems, rather than just a smart search engine. AI Mode has previously only been available in the US, the UK and India, but now Google has rolled it out to over 180 additional countries.

The news: Meta is offering AI translations for creators to expand their global reach.

Why it matters: Meta AI translations — a tool that dubs and lip-syncs reels on Facebook and Instagram into another language — will now be available for English to Spanish and Spanish to English translations, with further languages in the pipeline. The move has the potential to help creators grow audiences in new markets, boosting the creator economy even further.

The news: ChatGPT-5 launches for businesses.

Why it matters: Hot on the heels of OpenAI’s rollout of ChatGPT-5 to consumers and developers last week, the company has extended the model to its enterprise customers. Spanish bank BBVA and Zara owner Inditex have already adopted the updated tool — Inditex data and AI lead Oscar Mateos took to LinkedIn to say, “GPT-5 feels less like a tool and more like an expert collaborator who’s always one step ahead.” Who will be the first luxury conglomerate to adopt the upgraded tech?

The news: Stitch Fix announces AI shopping updates in personalisation push.

Why it matters: Stitch Fix is seeking a competitive edge as several dedicated, AI-powered personal styling startups burst onto the scene — including Daydream, which was founded by former Stitch Fix COO Julie Bornstein, and has so far raised $50 million in funding to support its development. Stitch Fix has previously deployed AI to understand personal style and predict trends, but claims that a new suite of AI-powered personal styling features will “increase personalisation, convenience and inspiration” for its users. The updated features include: an AI style assistant for customers, which uses generative AI to suggest outfit inspiration based on the taste profile it builds from their data over time; a “Stylist Connect” platform for customers to chat to human stylists; virtual try-on “personalised AI style visualisation”; and AI design integration for its private brands.

The news: OpenAI launches ChatGPT-5, touting its knowledge as a “major upgrade” from ChatGPT-4.

Why it matters: We’ve been waiting for this update for a while (the last GPT-4 update was in March 2023), and the developments within OpenAI’s technology are a key indicator of how far AI has come, and what brands should know it can do. In OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s words, “GPT-3 sort of felt like talking to a high school student, GPT-4, maybe it was like talking to a college student. But with GPT-5, now it’s like talking to an expert, a PhD-level expert in anything, any area you need, on demand.” OpenAI also says its new model beats the LLMs from competitors Google, X and Anthropic. Perhaps most interestingly for brands, Open AI says the new model is more conversational than ever, which could have implications for customer interactions with their brands both in ChatGPT search for shopping, and their chatbot interactions.

The news: Pinterest CEO pitches the platform as an “AI-enabled shopping assistant”.

Why it matters: In the company’s second-quarter earnings call, Pinterest CEO Bill Ready said the app’s users don’t necessarily think of it as a shopping platform, but that its experiments with AI mean they’re actually getting proactive recommendations for products that “align with their taste and their style, the way a really great personal shopping assistant would”. Ready said the platform is also using multimodal AI (combining text and images), AI for visual search, and AI for conversational search. It’s one to watch for brands, as consumers move to more niche social platforms for product discovery.

The news: Google says AI search is increasing, not decreasing, traffic to websites — but doesn’t share data to back up its claims.

Why it matters: Some industry analysts suggest that the rise in AI-powered conversational search is decreasing organic traffic to websites. This week, Google rebuffed these claims as “inaccurate”. “Average click quality has increased and we’re actually sending slightly more quality clicks to websites than a year ago (by quality clicks, we mean those where users don’t quickly click back — typically a signal that a user is interested in the website),” Google’s head of search Liz Reid wrote in a blog post. Yet the blog cited no data — and the reports it was challenging do. Google isn’t the only AI-powered search engine, either. ChatGPT is increasingly being used for consumers’ shopping searches. AI optimisation is emerging among marketers to try to increase their sites’ chances of appearing in search — here’s what brands need to know about the nascent practice.

The news: Mark Zuckerberg says those without AI smart glasses will be at a “significant cognitive disadvantage” in future.

Why it matters: Meta had a big week last week, beating revenue and profit expectations in its second-quarter earnings. It’s good news for CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who has been investing heavily in AI, and will be wanting to reassure investors that the company is in a position to do so. Zuckerberg seized the good news opportunity to go in even harder on the company’s AI ambitions. Not only did he announce that the company’s AI models will soon reach human-like “superintelligence”, but he reinforced his belief that AI-powered glasses will be the primary way humans interact with AI in coming years.

“I continue to think that glasses are basically going to be the ideal form factor for AI," Zuckerberg told investors on the earnings call. “I think in the future, if you don’t have glasses that have AI — or some way to interact with AI — you’re probably going to be at a pretty significant cognitive disadvantage.” Meta has something of a first-mover advantage in the world of smart glasses, but Google, OpenAI and Apple are among the other Big Tech players investing in wearables’ AI promise. Read more about Meta’s smart glasses moves here.

The news: Experts say AI is developing much faster than expected.

Why it matters: We’re used to tech CEOs shouting about the potential of AI. But when experts including Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton say the technology is developing much faster than they ever anticipated, it adds even more fuel to the fire. Examples of AI models’ accelerating developments are everywhere: this week, Meta’s model began correcting itself.

Since Trump more or less deregulated the sector in the US, there’s barely anything standing in these companies’ way. This means global brands need to get to work on developing internal AI guardrails, especially if they’re handling lots of consumer data across jurisdictions (like the EU) that are stricter on AI.

The news: Apple says it is “very open” to acquisitions this year to catch up to competitors on AI.

The news: Google launches AI shopping mode in the UK.

Why it matters: Google launched its AI Mode search feature for shopping in the US in May, and the UK rollout this week indicates its plans to expand the number of consumers who shop using the feature — and fast. AI Mode uses Google’s generative AI tool to produce a chat-style interface for users, giving them a conversational search experience in which they can converse back and forth, and ask more specific questions. Three other AI shopping features rolled out on Google in the US — virtual try-on, Gemini-powered personalised shopping recommendations, and agentic price-match comparisons — are yet to be announced in the UK.

It’s particularly relevant for shopping. Some 80 per cent of consumers now rely on AI-written results for at least 40 per cent of their searches, according to Bain & Co. All this means ad agencies and marketing teams have shifted their focuses from SEO (search engine optimisation) to what’s been coined “AIO” (AI optimisation). Learn more about emerging AIO practices in fashion here.

The news: UK government signs “strategic partnership” with OpenAI in AI investment push.

Why it matters: The UK is eager not to get left behind in the so-called ‘AI race’ between the US, Europe and China, and this is the latest sign it’s keen to attract more investment to Britain’s AI sector. The government’s plans to use more of OpenAI’s technology to deliver public services will likely mean that the technology is trained on citizen data. In turn, OpenAI is planning on hiring more UK staff for its research and engineering teams, and increasing the size of its London office, as per the plan. ChatGPT maker OpenAI is currently one of the most powerful companies in the world, and President Trump’s new AI Action Plan shows how eager each government is to persuade the tech company — and its competitors — to develop their tech on their soil.

The news: Trump unveils US AI Action Plan and signs three AI executive orders.

Why it matters: The 28-page ‘AI Action Plan’ aims to build out the country’s AI infrastructure, cement America’s dominance in the industry and prohibit all federal agencies from using AI contractors that don’t comply with the White House’s definition of “ideological neutrality”. The new policies reverse several Biden-era federal AI safeguards related to DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) and climate change, block state-level regulations on AI and further relax export rules so that global companies rely deeper on US-built AI. The move to get rid of existing AI regulations places further onus on individual companies to establish their own AI guardrails, especially if they operate across countries and jurisdictions. The US-centric policy also presents key challenges for fashion’s global supply chain and consumer base, which you can read more about here.

The news: OpenAI has shown some brands a pilot of a checkout feature that would enable users to complete purchases within its ChatGPT platform, according to a report by the Financial Times. It would charge brands commission for sales made this way.

Why it matters: When users search for products, ChatGPT currently shows recommendations with links to click through to brands’ own e-commerce sites. Bypassing this step opens up a clear revenue stream for OpenAI, but could significantly impact brands’ online sales. Those whose websites are picked up easier by ChatGPT would hold a significant advantage over those whose aren’t. No one’s quite sure what makes large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT tick yet, but there are some key practices emerging that could help brands optimise for AI search.

The news: WeTransfer has U-turned on plans to use UGC to train AI, after a revision in its terms of service caused widespread backlash.

Why it matters: Copyright protection has long been in place to safeguard creatives like photographers against their work being used without permission. Tech companies’ training of AI models on their work is proving a thorny issue within the fashion and creative industries, as it poses a risk of copies, duplication and direct competition — ultimately threatening their source of income. Given that WeTransfer is widely used within the creative industries, the company’s U-turn represents the perceived reputational risk that openly training AI models on creative work can cause.

The news: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said the company will build a data centre “the size of Manhattan” to fuel its planned development of AI products.

Why it matters: It’s the latest in a string of moves from Meta — which owns Instagram, Whatsapp and Facebook — that demonstrate the scale of the investment it’s making in developing AI products. Data centres are hugely expensive to build and maintain, and the size of what Zuckerberg is suggesting would cost billions of dollars. Zuckerberg has been very bullish on the potential for the company’s AI smart glasses in particular, and talk of Meta buying a stake in its Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses co-creator EssilorLuxottica has intensified in the last month.

A lucky few will join us Tuesday, November 10th at the newly opened, architecturally stunning Lucas Museum of Narrative History to honor Denis Villeneuve, GQ’s Director of the Year. #6701. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#6700. Dia Art Foundation and Chanel Celebrate Steve McQueen and Roni Horn

Sofia Coppola, Julio Torres, and Marion Cotillard also attended the gala.

As co-chairs of Dia Fall Night 2026, Carrie Mae Weems, Rosemarie Trockel, and Matthieu Blazy hosted an amazing roster of guests to celebrate the Dia Art Foundation’s initiatives. Sofia Coppola, Marion Cotillard, Julio Torres, and artists Chase Hall, Marina Abramović, Garrett Bradley, and Cecily Brown were among those who turned out for the Chanel-sponsored event, which honored artists Steve McQueen and Roni Horn. Both McQueen and Horn have created installations shown at Dia Beacon, Dia’s most well-known exhibition space. It also served as a goodbye to Dia director Jessica Morgan, who will leave the organization after over a decade to serve as director of the Tate.

The evening began at Dia’s Chelsea galleries, where the show “David Lamelas: The Machine” was on display. Guests then made their way north a few blocks for cocktails and dinner. During the meal, artist Matthew Barney introduced Horn, his longtime friend, and reflected on a memory of explaining her work to his young daughter. In tribute to McQueen, musician and poet Meshell Ndegeocello made her way around the room performing a hymn and a striking spoken-word piece. (She collaborated with McQueen on the sound component of his 2024 Dia Beacon work “Bass.”) She was accompanied by singers Jade Hicks and Marsha Deboe and guitarist Chris Bruce.

Chanel and Blazy’s partnership with Dia is part of the brand’s continued support of arts organizations, which includes working with museums like the National Portrait Gallery in London and the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

Check out some of the starry art world attendees below.

Adrienne Gaffney is a features editor at ELLE and previously worked at WSJ Magazine and Vanity Fair.

#6699. 69 of the Best Kendall Jenner Street Style Looks

Kendall Jenner was first thrust into the public eye nearly two decades ago, as the quiet, tomboyish 11-year-old younger sister on Keeping Up With the Kardashians. But in 2014, the second-youngest member of the Kar-Jenner dynasty struck out to forge her own path as a model. Since her runway debut for Marc Jacobs’ fall 2014 show, Jenner has become a ubiquitous presence, not only on our TV screens, but on the runway and in magazines, too. With such a jam-packed schedule, the budding model became a regular street style subject, as she bounced from show to show.

Early photos captured Jenner’s style at the beginning of its evolution. Even at 19, she shows the same fashion DNA that she has today: a love of simplicity. As she’s become more entrenched in the fashion world, her interest in fashion history has broadened, as has her wardrobe. Case in point: these days, you can find Jenner mixing Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel with The Row or showing off her latest vintage Mugler grail.

Over the last 10 years, Kendall Jenner has gone from nascent model to fashion fiend. Below, in honor of the model’s birthday, revisit some of her best street style looks from 2014 until now.

Wearing a Phoebe Philo coat in Greenwich Village, 2025.

Celebrating her October 2025 Vogue cover.

At the Kylie Cosmetics 10-year anniversary party, 2025.

Wearing vintage Mugler in New York, 2026.

#6697. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6696. Owen Wilson Breaks Down the World’s Best Golf Courses

The PGA Tour may be wrapping up in just a few short weeks, but this week marks the official beginning of Stick Season. No, not the Noah Kahan song, but Owen Wilson’s charming Apple TV+ comedy, whose second season premieres this Wednesday, November 4th. The show follows Wilson’s Pryce “Stick” Cahill, a former pro golfer who crashed out in a Kenny Powers-esque blaze of almost-glory a couple decades ago. Season one tracked his reentry into the game as the mentor of a talented but troubled young golfer played by Peter Dager. But in Season two, Stick has his eyes on a new prize: becoming the oldest player to ever win the U.S. Open.

Wilson himself might not be winning majors any time soon, but his experience filming the show has turned him into a real golf nut. He hadn’t played much beforehand, he told me, so the last couple of years have been a real crash course in one of the most difficult sports in the world. Still, it hasn’t taken much for him to compile a list of his favorite courses—and a bucket list of ones he’s dying to play a round or two on. Ahead of the show’s return, the 57-year-old actor hit the links with GQ.

“I have gotten an invite from a member to play, so I think that will happen at some point. What's always funny about that is that they close right after The Masters, so they're closed all summer. I’ve got to find a time that works for them where I could go play. That would be incredible.”

“My brother says St. Andrews and some of the other courses in Scotland are incredible. Out there the links style is pretty different from the courses in Dallas. And the people in Scotland, Luke says, are so knowledgeable about the game and friendly. I have not played link style and sometimes I wonder, Well, maybe my game would suit that because sometimes I'm not getting a lot of lift on the ball. And I am very comfortable with a putter. So yeah, maybe that's where I'll really prove that I'm good at the game.”

“Playing in Makena on Maui, that's a beautiful course that I love playing where you're getting to see the ocean and the beautiful Hawaiian features.”

“I played this one in Sydney that's kind of their [version of] Pebble Beach. It’s on the ocean, and there are some dramatic holes where you see waves breaking. I played lousy that day, but I'd like another crack at it.”

“I remember asking Collin Morikawa what his favorite course was and he said Riviera. Getting to play Riviera, I kind of feel like I've gotten to know more about the game. In the beginning, it was sort of lost on me—like getting a really good bottle of wine, and I couldn't really tell the difference. But now that I'm getting better, I can appreciate how incredible that course is. That first hole, where you're kind of teeing off from way up above. Just the other day, on number 10, I had a par four where I drove the green and just barely made it to the front of the green. But I was immediately on the phone calling to let my brothers and friends know that I had an eagle putt, which I missed. But that kind of kicked off a good little stretch where I birdied three out of four holes. That was a rare kind of day. More often, I'm kind of experiencing how challenging golf is.”

“I’ve stayed [at the Manor] and the course where they’re going to hold the Ryder Cup next year looked beautiful.”

“When I was training for the show, I learned how to play at Maui Country Club, a little nine-hole course kind of near where I am on the North Shore. [Maui] and Mākena, those were the two places that I really played a lot.”

“I played my best round at King Kamehameha with [former NBA coach] Don Nelson. I'd only been playing for a year-and-a-half where I was able to shoot in the low 80s, and everything just was very simple that day. Like, you hit your drive on the fairway, and then on the fairway you just hit it on the green, and then you two-putt and move on. I was with Nellie when he got his last hole in one. At that point I think he was maybe 83, and he was able to shoot his age and get a hole in one. I have not gotten a hole in one yet, but it's very exciting to witness one.”

#6693. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6692. The 77 Best Red-Carpet Looks of All Time (and What You Can Learn From Them)

What does it mean to truly own the red carpet? It means showing out the way that stars have at the biggest events on the planet for generations now: In the swankiest, swerviest, most spotlight-stealing fashion possible.

Maybe that’s stunting in a disco-tinged jumpsuit like a ruffled John Malkovich at the 2026 Venice Film Festival, suiting up in sumptuous red velvet like Gwenyth Paltrow in 1999, keeping things simmeringly subtle like Frank Ocean’s Prada look at the 2019 Met Gala, or popping out the big lapels on a suede tux like Tom Holland at GQ’s Men of the Year 2021. Whatever your interpretation, the best red-carpet looks need to feel unexpected, look unforgettable, and radiate confidence.

To help jumpstart your own legendary party ensembles, here are 77 of the greatest red-carpet moments ever—and what you can learn from each.

Don’t be afraid to lean into your sex appeal.

As one wise Twitter user once put it, “Colman Domingo always dresses like he's stepped out of a GQ Mag shoot.”

This lush Gucci velvet suit became so instantly legendary that Gwenyth herself recreated the look more than 20 years later.

Frank caused some consternation (though not around these parts) when he showed up to 2019’s camp-themed Met Gala in an understated, decidedly un-camp look. Four years on, though, his outfit remains a great reminder that sticking to the classics—in this case, black-and-white Prada from head to toe—is never a poor choice.

Ruffles have ridges, and so does this suit.

Leaning retro can sometimes go awry on the red carpet, but Stanfield managed to pull the ‘70s look off with funky ease when he pulled this giant-collared, razor-sharp Saint Laurent jumpsuit out for the Oscars.

This outfit looks like it comes with its own walk-in music, and it’s loud.

The right to rock bare-chested suit isn’t something you demand—it’s something you earn.

Julia Effin’ Roberts in a Big Effin’ Suit. That’s it. That’s the caption.

Wearing Prada, like Wright at the 2023 Golden Globes, is a surefire way to get a lot of compliments. The brand makes you look stylish and smart. Don’t you just want to ask Wright which local art gallery to visit?

Gerber’s disco-ball gown is stunning, but it’s Butler’s silky, sumptuous, pussy-bow blouse—designed by Saint Laurent, as was his exquisitely tailored tux—that utterly steals the show.

#6690. Jenny Kee and the Untold Story of Chanel’s Original Australian Debut

It's everything that anyone who loves fashion Down Under can talk about right now: when Matthieu Blazy brings his resort collection to Sydney this November, it will be the first time Chanel has ever shown in Australia.

What relatively few people know, however, is that this landmark moment will not, by a long shot, be the first time Australia has shown in Chanel.

That moment happened 44 years ago, on October 18, 1982, at the Louvre in Paris. Halfway through a Chanel show that, until then, had been dominated by powerfully pastel and friskily high-hemmed interpretations of Coco Chanel’s canonical bouclé suit, something never before seen began to appear on the models who walked out in front of a line of Chanel-branded wardrobes.

It was a print, mostly on white, but sometimes on black, composed of an apparently haphazard accumulation of shapes. Their interiors were fractured into visually immersive pools and veins of cobalt, scarlet, yellow and blue. This pattern appeared first in flashes, then took over entire dresses, as well as jackets, bags, shoes and more. And then, on one white background ruffle-detailed dress, the apparent abstraction resolved itself into something very tangible: across a model’s torso ran the unmistakable outline of Australia.

Chanel spring/summer ’83 with a Kee print showing an outline of Australia. Image credit: Getty Images.

The print was the creation of the then-35-year-old Bondi-born fashion trailblazer Jenny Kee, who is of Chinese, Italian and English heritage, and deeply Australian in sensibility. Kee has been acknowledged in the past—not least, and quite rightly, by herself—as the author of the prints Chanel used that season. In 1983, the year of Coco Chanel’s centenary, the house presented, through Vogue Australia, a Chanel suit featuring Kee’s Opal print in the lining and lapels to the National Gallery of Victoria, where it is displayed online with full and correct attribution.

Yet the story of how an Australian designer came to play a key role in a Chanel collection that, despite being largely forgotten, was one of the most significant in its entire history has, until now, never been fully told. Fashion moves fast and always faces forward; unless preserved, details will fall away as freely as loosely applied sequins from a dress in motion.

Back in 1982, I was living with my mother in the Blue Mountains, where Kee was a neighbour and close family friend. Her brush with Chanel was probably the first fashion story I ever encountered. So, to mark Blazy’s arrival in Sydney, I decided to try to piece it back together and, in the process, discovered a few details even Kee herself was unaware of. As she said when I called her at home up in the mountains this October: “Darl, I had no bloody idea!”

Unlocking the circumstances behind Kee’s cameo for Chanel takes us first to London, where, by 1968, she was living. That December, she appeared naked on the cover of Oz magazine—edited by my late uncle Richard Neville—while working with fellow Australian Vernon Lambert, the visionary vintage dealer whose stall at the Chelsea Antique Market on the King’s Road was helping to rewrite the rules of fashion. Lambert was Kee’s mentor, and when she returned to Australia in 1972, she was ready to start something new.

She opened the Flamingo Park Frock Salon in Sydney’s Strand Arcade and, together with Linda Jackson, began building a fashion language whose point of reference was Australia itself: its opals, native flowers, fauna, bushfires, rainforests and the Great Barrier Reef. “We were doing a completely Australian beauty,” she says. “We were so fresh and so completely pure and so in love with Australia. We were devoted to our country and making beauty of it.”

Chanel spring/summer’83. Image credit: Getty Images.

When Kee and Jackson took that work to Milan in 1977, it caused a sensation. Kee remembers arriving at a party thrown by the Italian stylist and publicist Nally Bellati: “Linda and I walked in and, honestly and truly, they all started jumping on the tables and clapping us, because they’d never seen anything like it,” Kee recalls.

Among those who applauded was Anna Piaggi, the Italian fashion editor who happened to be another one of Lambert’s protégées. In a 1977 issue of Vogue Italia, Piaggi dedicated a double-page spread to Kee and Jackson’s designs under the headline: ‘Fashion arrived from another hemisphere.’ “Anna was bedazzled by what Linda and I were doing back in Australia,” says Kee. The article was accompanied by a sketch of Piaggi wearing Kee’s wool designs—it was drawn by Karl Lagerfeld.

Vogue Italia 1977 featured Kee in her own designs, along with Linda Jackson. Image credit: courtesy Vogue Italia.

Piaggi and Lambert were extremely close to Lagerfeld, who was inspired by Lambert’s habit of always carrying a vintage fan and regularly drew the elaborate outfits Piaggi assembled each day. Kee was entering a tight creative orbit whose members were already constantly looking at, wearing and exchanging one another’s discoveries. In 1977, Kee and her 22-month-old daughter Grace—my oldest friend—were also on a train between Sydney and the Blue Mountains that crashed, killing 83 of their fellow passengers. During their recovery from that neardeath experience, Kee was inspired to sketch Opal and several of her other most famous designs.

Back in Milan in 1980, Kee remembers showing these designs at the home of Piaggi and Lambert, with Manolo Blahnik also present. Lambert then introduced her to Fabio Bellotti of Rainbow Fabrics in Milan. As Kee’s graphics became too detailed and elaborate to realise in knitwear alone, Bellotti—who had long worked with designers including Giorgio Armani and Lagerfeld—was the perfect partner for transferring those designs into print.

Jenny Kee with Fabio Bellotti of Rainbow Fabrics in the 1980s. Image credit: courtesy Jenny Kee.

One of those designs was Opal. Developed around the shimmering colours and fractured structures of the Australian gemstone, it became central to Kee and Jackson’s 1981 Flaming Opal collection. This was the print that eventually caught Lagerfeld’s eye one day when he was in the Rainbow Fabrics office looking for fabrics for a very important new collection.

Daniela Morera, Bellotti’s wife, remembers Lagerfeld encountering Kee’s samples through her husband. “Karl fell in love,” she says of the Opal design. Like Kee, she also suggests that Piaggi and Lambert may have helped draw Lagerfeld’s attention to her work.

Kee remembers what happened next very clearly. Bellotti called her in Australia to say Lagerfeld wanted to use the print for Chanel. She immediately agreed. “Apparently, when Karl saw Opal, that’s when he went, ‘Bingo, I want that,’” she says. “And then he proceeded to do it in 65 different ways.”

By October 1982, Chanel itself was in transition. The house had launched ready-to-wear under Philippe Guibourgé in 1978, but its owner, Alain Wertheimer, was already looking for a designer who could rejuvenate a fashion image that had become dusty and out of touch following the death of Coco Chanel in 1971 and amid the emergence of the Japanese new wave and homegrown upstarts such as Jean Paul Gaultier. Wertheimer’s eye settled on Lagerfeld and, in September 1982, Chanel announced that Lagerfeld would become its designer of couture, starting in January 1983. According to MarieLouise de Clermont-Tonnerre, then a senior Chanel communications executive, Lagerfeld ghost-designed the October 1982 collection, with Hervé Léger and Eva Campocasso—previously both assistants of Lagerfeld at Fendi and Chloé respectively—serving as its public-facing designers as his contract with Chloé wound down.

Vernon Lambert in Rome in the early 1980s with Chanel bag and shoes using Kee’s prints from spring/summer ’83. Image credit: courtesy Jenny Kee.

This subterfuge was only casually maintained. Writing in The New York Times on the day of the show, Bernadine Morris reported: “Merely a whisper of a Karl Lagerfeld connection was enough to bring out the crowds and the tension … it has been rumoured that he had something to do with the ready-to-wear presented this morning as part of the spring and summer showings here … The Lagerfeld touch seems apparent in the pearl earrings in the shape of the numbers 5 and 19, both names of Chanel perfumes. For the rest, no-one is saying just how much he did. ‘Consultant’ is as far as his friends will go.”

Back in Blackheath, Kee had no idea any of this was happening. When I tell her that the Chanel collection in which her Opal print appeared was, in effect, Lagerfeld’s covert first act for the house, she laughs. “Darl, I had no bloody idea!” Then, delighted: “I love the fact he was ghosting it. It makes it even more interesting—and it means that my print played a part in his first-ever work for Chanel.”

I also show her a picture from a misdated cache of runway images that appears to show a second Kee print, Mali Oz, on the Chanel runway in a dress and handbag worn with an Opal jacket. Kee is astonished. “I’ve never seen that before!” she says. The National Gallery of Australia records that Chanel also used Kee’s Mali Oz fabric.

Whatever the details, Kee’s role also hints at Lagerfeld’s larger creative project: keeping the codes of Chanel intact while applying startling points of difference to push them into another register. “He thought, I’ll just do something really outrageous here,” Kee says, remembering the collision of her print with “that pale pink, old-fashioned Chanel”.

The result changed Kee’s life. “It helped me enormously,” she says. “In that one year, 1982, I was showing at Chanel, and a few months earlier Princess Di was wearing my koala jumper. So those two moments really helped set me on the road. I’m eternally grateful to Chanel and Karl, to Fabio and Daniela, to Anna and Vern. One way or another, they all helped lift me up.”

The Kee Chanel connection was well reported in Australia at the time, and cemented by the Vogue Australia-facilitated Chanel x Kee donation to the NGV. Outside of Australia, however, the strongest contemporary credit to Kee was delivered by another old friend, photographer Bill Cunningham, who dedicated one of his New York Times pages in August 1984 to Kee’s designs for Chanel citing her prominently. One of his photographs was of then Chanel American president Kitty D’Alessio wearing a Kee/Lagerfeld/Chanel spring/summer ’83 jacket. The page features Kee’s Opal and Mali Oz prints on Chanel pieces.

A Chanel jacket lined with Kee’s Opal print from Chanel spring/summer ’83. Image credit: Courtesy Jenny Kee. Powerhouse Collection. Purchased 1999. Photograph Nitsa Yioupros

Nearly half a century later, Chanel is finally touching down in the country that inspired the prints in the first collection Lagerfeld created as he set the house towards its current position at the pinnacle of fashion. Kee is a huge fan of Blazy. “I love his work,” she says. “He’s really standing up to Karl and doing his own thing now.” Coming from Kee—a woman who has spent her very big life doing her very unique thing—that is high praise indeed.

This story appears in Vogue Australia’s November 2026 issue, on sale from November 2.

#6689. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6687. 16 Best Automatic Watches for Men 2026, According to GQ Watch Nerds

A budding “watch guy” most likely starts off their collection with an assortment of quartz tickers (and let’s be clear, there’s nothing wrong with that). But as your interest in watches grows, it’s only natural for you to want something on your wrist you can brag about, which inevitably pushes you towards automatic watches.

Inside the case of an automatic watch is a weighted rotor that spins as you move your arm, a few little flicks of your wrist throughout the day keeps the internal mechanisms running long enough to keep that minute hand tick-tick-ticking across the dial.

But automatic watches also have a reputation for being finicky or costly. And while that can be true, the beauty of watches is the wide price scale in which the industry operates. From stunners for less than $250 to ones you’d have to mortgage your house (and maybe your parents’ house) to buy, here are the top automatic watches on the market today for any budget.

While not impossible to find a great watch at the $250-mark, you are going to be limited. Given the many internal pieces and complicated mechanisms needed to build an automatic watch, many brands have to charge a bit more for a quality automatic. Even so, brands like Orient and Seiko lead the way on well-made (and well-designed) options.

Orient’s range of inexpensive watches punch well above their weight-class and the Symphony III is no different. With its classic, clean design and movement that promises 40 hours of power reserve, this is a watch that’s made to be a daily driver without breaking the bank.

Timex’s Waterbury is a staple in their line-up and the extremely stylish Metrograph has an Art Deco-style case and dial that’s pared-down enough to keep things simple, but without looking boring.

The Seiko 5 is something of a cult favorite for the Japanese brand – and for good reason. It’s a perfect daily driver and a budget-friendly alternative to the Rolex Datejust. Best of all, it clocks in at just 37mm, which is the perfect case size for nearly any wrist.

As ever, Timex provides maximum bang for minimum buck with this classic "Pepsi" bezel diver.

At $500, the doorway starts to open up a bit more – but only a creak. The usual suspects like Timex and Casio, are populating this price point, Bulova and Sternglas are great alternatives who will give you a little more street cred among collectors.

Undoubtedly one of the best looking watches in the sub-$500 category, the Timex Marlin in this particular shade of green strikes the perfect balance between classic and modern.

Heavily influenced by motorsports, the Edifice is a bit of a departure from the digital, retro-charm of many mainstays for Casio. The integrated bracelet keeps it sporty, while the patterned dial makes it a little more interesting than other options on the market.

At 45mm, 200-meter of water resistance, and 42-hours of power reserve, the Bulova Marine Star ticks all the boxes for a great dive watch at a reasonable price – the two-toned bezel is just a nice bonus.

This fan favorite hits the bullseye of the style-quality-price nexus, and looks especially fetching with a bright yellow dial.

A thousand bucks is a perfectly reasonable budget to have when you want to upgrade your watch game without completely breaking the bank. Here, I’d recommend looking at smaller, or more indie brands to find some interesting designs not seen by more household names.

You’d be forgiven for not knowing their name, but Kuoe is starting to gain traction in the U.S.. The Japanese-based watchmaker produces high-quality, well-designed pieces that harken to a more classic watch style. The OLD SMITH is based on the military field watch, but with a slightly more refined design language.

A reborn grail from the Studio 54 era, with a vintage-correct 35mm case.

UNIMATIC uses the basic field watch as the springboard for their Modello Due, which strips it back to its barebones to make something a bit bolder, a bit more modern, and eye-catching.

Paulin is a Glasgow-based microbrand that’s known for colorful, unique, and whimsical watches, often playing with color to make their designs all the more interesting.

Needless to say, if money isn’t an issue, the sky’s the limit. Not all watches are created equal and buying just for the name recognition alone doesn’t always make for the best watch for the money. Instead, look for a price point that’s commensurate with the movement, design, and materials used, and you’ll never regret the decision to spend the big bucks.

Taken from a 1924 archival design, the Brunswick’s cushion case, clean lines, and mother-of-pearl dial may all feel a bit “precious”, shall we say; but this is a workhorse watch that’s destined to be a daily driver for anyone who is looking for a little eye-candy on the wrist.

The IWC Ingenieur is a masterfully made ceramic watch (and matching ceramic bracelet) that will no doubt get you a few compliments every time you wear it to the office.

Not many watches can be mistaken for a Bell & Ross watch with its larger proportions and signature square case shape. The BR-05, the brand’s most popular model, is a sportier, slightly bolder answer to Cartier’s Santos.

It’s hard to narrow down one Grand Seiko to choose, but the White Birch is subtle and versatile enough to dress up or use as your daily driver. Most impressive about this particular model is the Caliber 9SA5 movement, which promises a whopping 80-hours of power when fully wound – nearly twice that of many others on the market.

Mechanical watch movements fall into two basic categories: hand-wound and automatic. Before the invention of automatic wristwatches in the 1920s (and long before the invention of battery-powered quartz movements in the 1960s) all watches were hand-wound. That meant you needed to manually wind up your watch every day to keep it running. An automatic watch (also called a self-winding watch) doesn’t require this because it winds automatically with the movement of your body as you wear it.

Most automatic watches wind themselves via a weighted rotor, which you’ll be able to see if your watch has a see-through case back (it’s the half moon-shaped piece right on top). When you wear the watch and move around, the rotor winds a spring, which turns the hands, date wheel and everything else that moves on a watch.

To keep your watch from stopping when you’re sitting still (or when you take it off at night) automatic movements also store excess energy and slowly release it over hours or days while the rotor is stationary. This is called a “power reserve,” and it typically ranges from 40 to 80 hours, with some going as high as a week or more. They’re useful if you don’t wear a watch every day, and don’t want to have to reset the date and time every time you put it on—particularly with annual or perpetual calendar models that can be complicated to set.

It’s not a downside, per se, but they do require some upkeep. Unlike a quartz watch that requires nothing more than a new battery every few years, a mechanical watch is a finely-tuned machine consisting of many tiny, precisely calibrated parts. Watchmakers have made huge advances in shock-and waterproofing over the years, but there’s still only so much abuse a mechanical movement can take. And that’s the thing: repairs to automatic watches can be expensive.

If you stick to the manufacturer’s recommended service schedule (it’ll need an overhaul and lube every 4 to 10 years, depending on the brand and model) and don’t make a habit of wearing it in the sauna, you’ll probably be fine. Whether it’s a $200 Amazon special or a $200,000 grand complication, automatic watches are designed to be worn, so the best way to take care of your watch is to wear it as much as possible.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6686. The Easiest Exercise for Longevity, According to Science

A few months ago, I had never so much as lifted a barbell—let alone thought about exercises for longevity. However, during a stay at Buchinger Wilhelmi Clinic, I attended a life-changing lecture by Felipe Isidro, a professor of physical education and CEO of Physical Exercise & Health Consulting. That was the day everything changed.

“Who here works out?” Isidro asked. “When I say ‘work out,’ I don’t mean normal physical activities like walking, climbing stairs, and carrying shopping bags. I mean ‘exercise,’ which is movement that is both planned and scheduled. I ask, because 7 out of 10 people don’t: That’s 70% of the population.”

Of course, any physical activity is better than none. “But you don’t get the same benefits as with exercise,” Isidro explained. “The ideal, instead, is to combine both—to move more on a daily basis and to set aside specific time for training. In a society that invites us to move less and less with cars, elevators, and escalators, the objective should be to exercise—and, especially, to do strength training.”

Up until then, I had never thought of the true importance of exercise: I’d only thought of it as a means to an end—to lose weight and, ideally, to look better in my clothes. Although it is true that exercise can help on both accounts, Isidro allowed me to see that neither of those are as important as keeping the body’s muscles and mitochondria healthy for as long as possible. “The mitochondria are like little batteries that produce the energy that impact vitality,” Isidro explained. “When the mitochondria work well, we feel strong; when they deteriorate, we feel fatigued. It’s also difficult to burn fat, even when we diet. Fat not only accumulates under the skin but also in organs, viscera, and even in the muscle itself.”

Here, there is no miracle pill—the only “medicine” proven to improve mitochondrial function is exercise, and especially strength training. Just as a cell phone battery lasts for hours when it’s new but loses its ability to hold a charge, the same thing happens with mitochondria—as we age, we may wake up with energy but feel exhausted by mid-morning. Thus, we must keep our mitochondria as healthy as possible.

Within the muscle there are slow twitch fibers and fast twitch fibers— slow twitch fibers are responsible for prolonged efforts such as walking; fast twitch fibers are essential for power and speed.

As we age, fast twitch fibers are the first to decline. “Walking improves endurance, but it doesn’t stop the loss of fast twitch fibers. If you don’t train strength, you become sluggish. We see it in older people, who end up walking in short steps because they have lost those fibers. Strength training is the only way to keep them,” Isidro points out. “We gain muscle until the age of 25, maintain it until the age of 35 and, from then on, we start to lose it slowly, accelerating from the age of 50, and even more at the age of 65. There are cases of people in their 70s who maintain the strength of someone sedentary in their 40s or 50s thanks to daily training, proving that this habit can subtract up to 20 years from biological age.”

After all, what you don’t use, you lose. That goes for muscle—but also for bones, the respiratory system, and the pelvic floor. Regular exercise also improves the non-REM phase (deep sleep in which the eyes do not move), and that also decreases with age. Having longer non-REM phases is related to gradual and healthy aging. “Strength training is an investment in health for the future,” Isidro says. “It reduces anxiety and it makes us feel better at all levels. In reality, a healthy body is a perfect body.”

While water is essential for our hydration, too much of it can cause us to drown. Strength training is similar: The proper dosage is key. It’s not about doing it in excess; it’s about doing it right. The right dose, says Isidro, means few repetitions, lots of recovery time, and, above all, not looking to fatigue: “Many people think that, if they don’t get tired, they haven’t trained properly. It’s actually just the opposite. In strength, we’re not looking to exhaust ourselves, we’re looking for quality.” To that end, here are seven points to keep in mind in order to strength train properly, no matter your age or fitness level.

The minimum for adaptation is two days a week, although the ideal scenario would be to progress to three or four with breaks in between—one day on, one day off. You should also do strength before endurance; if you do both on the same day, it’s best to finish with cardio.

If you’re new to working out, it’s best to focus on the legs. They are the largest reservoir of muscle mass in the body and also the quickest to deteriorate. In addition, the legs contain a lot of fast twitch fibers, so training them is vital.

Do reps at a high intensity (quickly) to work the fast twitch fibers. It is recommended to do a few repetitions—half or less of the maximum you can do—to avoid fatigue. “The key is speed and intensity, because that’s what activates the fast fibers through the nervous system,” says Isidro.

Give yourself plenty of time to rest between sets. At minimum, rest time should be one minute, but two or three minutes between exercises is even better. “You’re fully recovered when you can speak and sing, not just utter and grunt monosyllables,” says Isidro.

“It is essential that the exercise be non-exhausting or fatiguing. When you fatigue, you’re working the slow twitch fibers and continuing to lose fast twitch fibers,” says Isidro. “It’s better to do a few exercises well and repeat them a couple of times. Stop before fatigue sets in.”

Start with short workout sessions that last 5 to 15 minutes. Do them in a circuit format, alternating exercises with breaks. “We all have 10 minutes a day if we prioritize. Forget your previous experience—many of us think that exercise should be tiring and painful to work. If we do less, we enjoy it more and see the benefits, creating a positive ripple effect.”

Working the respiratory muscles is also essential, because it improves recovery and endurance. Take long, full breaths, breathing into the diaphragm.

According to Isidro, the best time to exercise is in the morning: “This stimulates the sympathetic system early, which makes it easier for the parasympathetic system to be stimulated in the evening, improving sleep.” If possible, exercise outdoors, because contact with nature and socialization have a direct effect on health.

You don’t need a full gym to get the benefits. Working out with your own body weight can be really effective. “The important thing is that the exercises are adapted to your fitness level so that you can repeat and maintain them over time,” Isidro says. “And if you can do them in a group or with friends, even better. Socializing motivates, engages, and, as studies show, lengthens life.”

There are several simple tests that can be done at home in order to check our current strength level and to show us where we may need to improve. “The important thing about these tests is not only to know where we are, but also to measure how we are progressing,” notes Isidro. “Sometimes the change is perceived in how we feel, but other times we need objective data, and these are very simple tools that allow us to tangibly see how strength training is helping us improve.” Below, some of those tests.

One useful test is to stand up and sit down five times as fast as possible using just your legs—all you need is a chair and a stopwatch. This test measures the strength of the legs, which is where we have the most muscle and, at the same time, where we usually lose muscle first.

This one combines strength and balance. It involves standing on the non-dominant leg and lifting the other leg. The goal is to maintain posture without using the arms. In people under 50 years of age, it is done with eyes closed, and in older people, with eyes open to prevent falls. The ideal is to balance for at least 45 seconds.

The six-minute endurance test involves walking as fast as possible for six minutes. Walking less than 500 meters indicates poor cardiorespiratory fitness; walking between 500 and 700 meters is acceptable; walking more than 700 is excellent.

Shawn G. Anthony, MD, an orthopedic sports medicine surgeon and associate system chief of sports medicine at Mount Sinai, says that almost every form of movement will help with longevity and has some value. But you shouldn’t rely on just one type of exercise to do everything. “There is no single longevity exercise,” Anthony says. “The goal is to build cardiovascular fitness and strength while preserving the ability to move well and remain active over time.”

He goes on to explain that the strongest evidence for longevity is combining aerobic exercise with resistance training. Think brisk walking, running, cycling, swimming, or sports with free weights, resistance bands, or body weight. With that in mind, here are some other exercises to consider.

Walking is one of the easiest exercises you can incorporate to daily life and is backed up by science. “It is accessible, low impact, and easy to sustain, and meaningful health benefits occur well below 10,000 steps per day,” Anthony explains. “There is also good evidence that walking after a meal can reduce the rise in blood glucose that follows eating, so even a brief post-meal walk can be a useful way to incorporate more movement into the day and improve metabolic health.”

He says that weighted walking can help. And while trendy walking exercises such as tai chi walking and lymphatic walking come with limited research in regards to longevity, anything that gets you moving is beneficial.

Picking up a new sport like tennis isn’t easy in the sense that you’ll get the hang of it in one (or even several) tries. But if you’re not trying to be the next Serena and just doing it for fun, it can be a form of exercise you look forward to. Anthony adds that sports can be especially useful because you train a lot of things at once, and one of the best examples is tennis. “It combines aerobic conditioning with bursts of higher-intensity movement, changes of direction, coordination, reaction time, and a social component,” he says. “Studies of racket sports have reported favorable associations with longevity.”

Yes, these workouts are hard. But finding a workout that you like and want to stick to will make it easy for you to meet your longevity goals. Anthony says that trendy workouts such as Pilates, HIIT, and Zone 2 training can be useful as long as the underlying training makes sense. You want to identify your fitness goals and find an exercise that will help you meet them safely and consistently. “If a trendy workout motivates someone to exercise regularly, that has real value,” he says. “What matters more than the label is whether the workout contributes to a well-rounded and sustainable exercise program.”

Anthony says to avoid anything that will repeatedly cause joint pain, tendon problems, or overuse injuries. “That is not a successful longevity strategy,” he says. “The goal is to increase physical capacity without repeatedly exceeding what the body can recover from.”

He also says that our fitness and strength are built up over time in our 20s, 30s, 40s, and 50s. So while it would be ideal to not wait until later in adulthood to begin thinking about longevity, starting now is still better than later (or never).

And just remember that the foundation of longevity remains regular aerobic exercise, resistance training, and daily movement. Whatever will get you those three will be the best workout for you. “Longevity requires durability,” he says. “Ultimately, the goal is to preserve enough physical capacity to keep running, skiing, playing tennis, traveling, and doing activities that matter to you 20 or 30 years from now.”
