#6685. Simu Liu’s First Favorite Brand Was Abercrombie & Fitch

Simu Liu is no stranger to fashion’s biggest night, so, when I met him at his hotel in SoHo Monday night, he figured the Council of Fashion Designers of America Awards show should be a cinch. “I think everything’s a little bit more chill than the Met Gala,” Liu says. “So I’m looking forward to having a little bit of a more relaxed environment to talk to fashion houses and meet people from the different brands and also just to see friends.”

We speak just a few hours before the 37-year-old actor is about to make his first appearance at the Oscars of fashion and it’s hard to tell that he just hopped off a plane from Los Angeles this morning. The Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings actor has had a packed year, from making his Broadway debut in Oh, Mary! between February and April to getting married back in October. He’s preparing to start promotion for the highly anticipated December release of Avengers: Doomsday, in which he’s set to reprise his role as the superhero Shang-Chi. Marvel fans haven’t seen him on the screen since his record-breaking film debut in 2021. “It’s been a long, long time,” he jokes.

For now, he’s clad in a robe sitting barefoot on the sofa, swiping a metallic device across his unblemished, glowing face. “I think it’s like a gua sha, but it’s cold,” he speculates. (His makeup artist, Alex Keating, confirms that it’s Shark Beauty’s Depuffi, a hot-and-cold contrast therapy gua sha that basically “gives you a full facial.”) A room service trolley is sitting inches away from him, allowing him quick access to a plate of chicken tenders and fries. And a Diet Coke. Don’t forget the Diet Coke.

Keating makes good use of Liu’s wavy locks, hairspraying a Superman-like curl into permanent place on his forehead as he sips his fridge cigarette. The actor’s dad cut his hair until he was 18 and he says it took him a while to learn what worked for his own mane. He envied the typical stick-straight Asian hair others had, but through his work with groomers learned the power of salt sprays to lean into his hair’s natural texture. It admittedly took a while for Liu to develop his own fashion sense as an adult, too.

“When you grow up working class and you grow up with parents whose purchasing habits were just the furthest thing from luxurious, I think it just takes time for you to learn about fashion,” he says. “The first brand that I remember really caring about was Abercrombie & Fitch.”

Tonight, though, Liu has moved far beyond the mall. He’s attending the CFDA Awards on behalf of White Rabbit Trust, an organization that supports AAPI creatives and entrepreneurs. It's hosting the award’s Emerging Designers Table, which allows industry leaders—this year, Jason Wu—to mentor AAPI designers who create custom looks for the muse of their choosing. In Liu’s case, he’s been dressed by Asian-Canadian designer Haoran Li of the brand Private Policy.

The look for the evening was a matching set made from black silk jacquard woven with bamboo paired with a shiny new silver wedding ring and a Rolex Batman GMT-Master II. His cropped trucker-style jacket, accented by hand-knotted Chinese buttons, sat over a crisp frayed-hem white button-down with wide-legged pants that draped over low-profile black shoes. “In Chinese culture, bamboo is one of the Four Gentlemen, a symbol of integrity and resilience,” Li says. “It bends in the storm but never breaks. That felt like Simu, who has spent his career pushing through doors that weren’t built for us.”

I ask if he’s ever bothered by the responsibility of representing the Asian diaspora. “Right around the time Crazy Rich Asians came out, it was the first studio Asian movie in 25 years,” he recalls. “Then Shang-Chi was the first Asian Marvel superhero movie. For a while it was just like first this, first this, first this. So I felt like innately the stakes were high and I put pressure on myself. I don’t regret doing that. I just remember looking around and not really seeing anyone doing that. So I thought, well it might as well be me.”

To that point, this isn’t the first time Liu has used his name to promote an indie AAPI brand. At the the premiere of Shang-Chi in 2021, he spotlighted Singaporean-British designer Chelsea Scott-Blackhall’s label Dzojchen, wearing the brand’s silk kimono tuxedo.

Prominence in Hollywood has meant more to him than giving him the opportunity to wear really nice clothes. He’s decided to take more agency in his career, he says. Last year, he starred and executive produced the spy thriller series The Copenhagen Test, which despite favorable reviews was cancelled after one season. That hasn’t slowed his aspirations for new creative outlets: "I think actually right now I’m really excited by the idea of becoming a director."

But before we get to see “Directed by Simu Liu” on the big screen, the star has an awards show to attend—and a plate of tendies to devour. Just as quickly as he’s touched down here in New York, he’s off again to Hong Kong tomorrow.

#6684. Cottage Cheese Meatballs and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

Call me a kindergartener, but lately my favorite sweet is a big crunchy-chewy cereal treat. Thank goodness my fellow Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk developed BA’s Best Rice Krispies Treats, complete with browned butter and unmelted mini marshmallows stirred in along with the melty sugar glue. I sometimes like to play and add a little drizzle of tahini or toasted nuts into the mix; but honestly nothing hits quite like a classic RKT. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

Remember the TikTok cucumber guy? He’s doing a collaboration with Chipotle now. What a time to be alive! To celebrate, I mandolined my stash of Persians, drizzled them with toasted sesame oil, seasoned them with salt and MSG and sriracha, dolloped them with mayo, then shook the hell out of them. The easiest, most satisfying way to eat a side salad. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO and cooking

The thing I miss most about living in a house instead of my city apartment is the ability to grill. I would grill at every meal if I could! But this week I made deputy food editor Hana Asbrink’s Gochujang Yogurt Chicken, and my craving for char was sated. She calls on you to broil, not bake, your chicken thighs which allow for the sugars in the gochujang to caramelize then burn to crispy perfection. Plus, this made enough for my household of two to enjoy the leftovers for two desk lunches. A definite win in my book. —Carly Westerfield, manager audience strategy

I did not plan to make an apple pie this week. I had plans to make salmon bowls, breakfast burritos, but no apple pie. Nevertheless, by some strange confluence of events that I still don’t quite understand, I found myself standing in front of an egg-washed, double-crusted, towering apple pie, crimping the edges of the dough. I followed the recipe for BA’s Best Apple Pie which has a rather long list of ingredients, and some steps that might seem unfamiliar to pie-heads, but in the end it’s worth the fuss. —Sam Stone, senior editor

My coworkers have jumped on the cottage cheese bandwagon and are sneaking the ingredient into everything: smoothies, lasagna, meatballs! I have fallen for every iteration. Keep ’em coming. But the meatballs? Now those are very special. Mixing the ground beef with cottage cheese seasons them with salty tang from the inside out. It also stretches the recipe, which means more meatballs (yay!). I ate them throughout the week with tangles of noodles, tucked into a sub for lunch, and mixed into a bracing salad. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Though I am a vegetarian chili gal myself, I just made a batch of pumpkin chili for a care package for a meat loving loved one. It has ground beef, two types of beans (I threw in lentils too), and instead of the typical tomato backdrop, a can of pumpkin purée for a glowing hue and squashy depth. I almost always double a soup recipe—more yield, barely more work—and I’m glad I did. Now I have a few extra containers in the freezer that’ll come in handy for a cold night down the road. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Also for the care package, I made a giant batch of Chickpea Saag. With frozen spinach and canned chickpeas, this recipe makes the most of ingredients I almost always have around. With rice, Greek yogurt, and lime wedges, it’s a cozy meal in its own right. But I like to sprinkle some feta on top just to gild the lily. —E.L.

I love hosting, but at the end of a long week, I need to maximize flavor and minimize dishes. That’s why I love this Spiced Red Rice Chicken recipe from Eden Eats. It allowed me to have everything prepped before guests arrived, so I could enjoy the hang and not fuss about timing. After seasoning chicken thighs generously with salt and letting them rest for 30 minutes, I seared them, set aside, and sautéed onions, garlic in all the flavor left over (I skipped the red pepper for one of my guests). I added additional spices and tomato paste and toasted the rice. I added chicken broth, placed the chicken back in skin side up, and tossed in some knobs of butter so the rice would crisp up nicely. Into the oven at 425 for 30 minutes, and it was yummy and convenient, not to mention a definite crowd-pleaser—and my dishwasher was happy! —Abi Lieff, assistant to the editor in chief

I’m not much of a pasta person. (I know, gasp!) But when fellow Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser first developed her Smashed Broccoli Pasta—a recipe that combines over a pound of broccoli with less than one pound of pasta—my heart opened up to the idea of making it for dinner. Her technique is genius, smashing broccoli into verdant rubble that burrows its way into tubular pasta. With not much more (just red pepper, garlic, and anchovies if you’re feeling frisky), you get a veggie-loaded, fiber-packed pasta in no time. Rebecca, thank you. Perhaps I will become a pasta convert. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

A fried fish sandwich has no season. Also, I’m currently in Tennessee, where it’s hit 90° this week, so it’s basically still summer. I used my colleague Shilpa Uskokovic’s excellent Fritto Misto batter to coat some flounder. After frying, I slid a couple small fillets into top-split hot dog buns with juicy slices of tomato and a quick tartar sauce. It was pure summer satisfaction, even this deep into October. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO and cooking

The days when my husband and I both commute are, to put it lightly, b-a-n-a-n-a-s. That’s when my deep freezer fulfills its destiny. Case in point: this superlative basil pesto, thawed overnight, tossed with hot rigatoni, plus frozen peas thrown in with the pasta for the last few minutes of boiling. It is nourishing and feels purposeful, even if it took less than 10 minutes of effort. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Andy Baraghani’s Honey-Chipotle Shrimp Tacos are one of my most-made recipes of all time. Last week I decided to change things up and eat the shrimp over some homemade Mexican rice and beans instead of wrapping them in a tortilla. The shrimp are so easy to make (just toss in a two-ingredient marinade and pan-fry) that I ended up cooking fresh batches for lunch on the following days to pair with the leftover rice and beans. The canned chipotles in adobo lend a smoky complexity, and I love how the honey helps the shrimp take on just enough char. A luxurious WFH lunch if there ever was one! —Alaina Chou, commerce writer

Soup on a weeknight? It’s a foreign concept to me. If I’m making soup, I’m committing hours to the cause. But this week I couldn’t quell my craving for a sippable bowl, so I scoured the archive for a quick hit and landed on this Curried Lentil, Tomato, and Coconut Soup. Red lentils break down and create a substantial body, while golden Japanese S&B curry powder adds a mellow earthy kick. After mixing in crushed tomatoes and coconut milk, I went rogue and followed up with a couple dashes of fish sauce for extra umami. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

The ever adaptable rotisserie chicken is one of my favorite emergency dinners. When crunched for time, I’ll grab one on my way home and transform the bird into something unrecognizable. Most recently, I used it to make Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser’s Nuoc Cham Chicken Salad. The pulled meat is tossed with the quickest mayo-lime dressing, then stuffed into lettuce leaves. I like to finish the cups with sliced cucumber, fried shallots, and a flurry of fresh herbs. Don’t bother bringing out plates. I eat this with my hands straight from the platter like nachos. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy

Whenever I want something more for breakfast, but I don’t want to work for it, it’s a Dutch baby all the way. Heat a skillet with butter, dump a couple of always-on-hand ingredients—eggs, flour, milk, sugar—into a blender, and 20 minutes later, it isn’t breakfast: It’s brunch. Last weekend I tossed the reserved browned butter from Epi’s Take It Easy Dutch Baby into a bowl of sliced Italian plums. I added a glug of maple syrup and a pinch of salt, then let the fruit soak in the flavors while I fiddled over my coffee. Puffed bébé out of the oven, the plums and all their juices went on top, and I sat down to enjoy my morning. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, cooking and SEO

I make lentil soup pretty frequently once the “feels like” temperature dips below 50 degrees. And I was just about to mince up my mirepoix when I stumbled upon senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic’s Soy-Braised Black Lentils. The promise of salty, tender-but-toothsome legumes on a bed of rice was good enough to shake up my routine. I hauled out my rice cooker, set it to steam, and started a dead-simple simmer of a pack of shiny black Beluga lentils with glugs of soy sauce and thin slices of garlic. Once the liquid was mostly gone, I stirred in glossy agave nectar plus added sugar until they formed a loose, syrupy glaze. We ate half the pot tucked into sheets of toasted seaweed snack along with generous spoonfuls of rice. The next morning, the rest was eaten with crusty bread and fried eggs. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

Ever since I started working at BA, I’ve seen this single recipe for Bolognese top the charts time and time again. An oldie but a baddie, it’s received over 500 comments that would taunt me on a daily basis, with one overall glaring thesis: Make this! Now! So I decided to hunker down, put on a killer album (Once in a Lifetime), and get comfortable in the kitchen. Yes, this Bolognese takes time—cough cough, three hours—but so do all good things. For those who need immediate gratification, your kitchen will be awash in the savory, primal smells of browned beef and pancetta in just 10 minutes. After adding a good amount of liquid from wine, stock, and milk (in stages), then stirring, dancing, and stirring, it was finally time to serve my meaty sauce tangled with fat pappardelle and a charitable shower of Parmesan. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

When I saw a bunch of bright-eyed leeks at the farmers market from my favorite vendor, I knew just what to do with them: my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s cheesy baked pasta. It was one of those love-at-first-sight recipes for me in the Test Kitchen—somehow minimalist and dramatic at the same time. Save this one for a chilly night when you’re having friends over. The sauce uses a cup of white wine, so there’s most of a bottle left to enjoy with dinner. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been making a lot of solo dinners lately, and nine times out of ten that means I’m cooking an omelet. My version with fried shallot, apple, and Fontina cheese is a go-to—I wrote all about it for our series, Me, Myself, and Dinner—but if I haven’t gone grocery shopping, I’ll just cobble together fun stuff from my fridge. Some recent wins: chopped kimchi and yellow cheddar; spinach, feta, and dill; black beans, avocado, and salsa macha. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

This week I did something I haven’t done in years. I roasted a chicken. And it was revelatory. Not fussy. Easy! Rewarding. Inspired by the method in Kitty Cowles’s cookbook, I sprinkled the bird with salt and let it hang out in the fridge for a few hours. Then I rubbed it with olive oil, threw some lemon and garlic in the cavity, and roasted it as high as my oven would go, convection on. While the chicken was resting, its skin a golden crackle, I deglazed the pan juices with white wine, and let those simmer into a tangy gravy. Served with a salad, it was the coziest supper, even romantic if you ignore my toddler cooing. The next day, the carcass simmered in a pot of water with onion and ginger for a broth I’ll sip for days. The surplus meat has morphed into a rice bowl, towering sandwich, day care lunch box, 3 p.m. snack. And the joy from it all? Incalculable. —E.L.

I’m always on the hunt for a protein-rich, not-too-finicky dinner that I can pull together in a blip. It’s gotta taste good because I’ll probably cook it for five consecutive days, at which point I will tire of it and resume my hunt anew. Like sands through the hourglass, these are the recipes of our lives. This week I settled on customizable Soy-Glazed Salmon Bowls. Cook the salmon in that salty-sweet soy and honey sauce, throw it atop rice, and add whatever vegetables you have. This time, I went with shreddy carrots and cukes, plus some of those crispy sheets of nori that I used to scoop up bite after bite. —Sam Stone, senior editor

My very talented colleague Shilpa Uskokovic forever changed the way I cook ground chicken. She mixes the chicken with baking soda—yes, baking soda—for clusters of bouncy nubbins. Now, anytime a recipe calls for ground meat, I use this hack. This week’s victim: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps. It has a sweet, fiery sauce made from sriracha, brown sugar, soy, and fish sauce that deliberately clings to the juicy meat. I piled the chicken into butter lettuce with a squeeze of lime, and a handful of torn mint for freshness. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6682. Why I’m Wearing Nothing But Pajamas

Last March, the 20th to be exact, I decided I was never going to wear anything but pajamas again, day and night. That was the day my life changed forever. That was the day my husband, Tad, died.

Tad was the only thing I never wanted to return or take back. I’m impossible to please, impossible to buy a present for, but he never stopped trying. I had no doubt about him. We met nearly 40 years ago, when I interviewed him on January 27, 1987, at three o’clock in the afternoon. He sat on a sofa, a large, overstuffed pale-gray one, in his writing studio in New York. A year and a half later, I was sitting on that same sofa and his writing studio had become our apartment. After we married, we did everything together. Worked together, played together—​our work was our play—traveled together. That never stopped, until it did.

I suddenly had four children, from my age (then mid-30s) down to four years old, plus four ready-made grandchildren and two new sobriquets—belle-mère and GrandDodie. (This was Tad’s way of easing me into early onset grandmotherhood and keeping that awful word stepmother from floating into my life.) Happily, none of the dear ones have ever called me the evil S-word, exceptfor one time on our way out to Quogue on Long Island on a summer weekend. Trying to keep cool on a hot Friday night, I’d tied my long dark hair in a knot at the top of my head. “Ooooohhhh,” Tad’s five-year-old daughter, Sarah, screeched from the back seat of our tiny Fiat convertible, where she was squished comfortably on her rocking horse. “The wicked stepmother!” There it was, out in the open.

But I stray. Pajamas. Or is it pyjamas? I like the word spelled the way the Brits do it, but feel it’s worthy of two spellings, like doughnut and donut. Either is better than the humiliating nicknames—pj’s, jammies, or jam-jams.

Pajamas—I’m going to live in them, go everywhere in them, never wear anything else. If Julian Schnabel can do it, why can’t I? Pajamas are for wearing inside, but when I feel up to going out again, I’ll wear them outside too. One night, I got a glimpse of my oldest stepdaughter, Trippy, wearing a pair in navy with white piping. I like that look. I filed the thought away. But the notion to live in pajamas hit me over the head when Tad’s niece Torrie drove me up to our house in Newport a week after Tad died. As soon as we arrived, in the middle of the afternoon, Torrie changed into the most delicious, crisp pair of navy-trimmed white-poplin Matouks. That was it. It was pajamas forever for me.

I might have mentioned my pajama game plan to my Vogue editor, because a few days later, a box from Petite Plume arrived containing the perfect pair of tailored striped ones, blue and white, a long pant and a long-sleeve top, 100 percent cotton. Chloe, my six-foot-tall editor, is more of a nightgown person and says, “Pajamas are often not made for tall people. You end up with the pant leg an awkward length.” But I don’t feel sorry for Chloe—I’m envious of her glorious monumentality (I’m five feet two when I can stand up straight), and, anyway, she gets the best nightgowns from Salter House in Brooklyn, spun from the finest cotton in all of Western Christendom.

My new pajamas are size extra-extra small and they fit just right, which means with a very loose and baggy ankle-​length pant. Webster’s defines pajamas as “worn for sleeping or lounging, typically consisting of a jacket or top and matching trousers.” The word dates back to the 19th century, derived from the Hindi term (also pājāma), which in turn comes from the Persian words pā for “leg” and jāma for “garment.” The pajama pant has long been worn throughout Asia as everyday wear, well before they became the sleeping-and-lounging uniform for every law-abiding Westerner.

I have no interest in lounging (loathe the word) and I’ll never wear them to bed. And it’s definitely not cool to wear the pajama top—pajama bottom or no pajama bottom. Pajama tops are like anchovies—they get pushed to the side of the plate. No one wants to wear just the top, except for maybe Ryan Gosling, who topped off a pair of crisp white pants with a white-piped pajama shirt at the Cannes Film Festival in 2011.

But bottoms are the tops for me, and for almost everyone I know. I’ve lived in my striped Petite Plume bottoms since the day they arrived last April. And not long ago, I found myself watching Doris Day in the 1957 movie The Pajama Game, where she worked in the Sleeptite Pajama Factory. “Wear Sleeptite at all social functions,” the workers sang. “Dresses are fine but Sleeptite’s divine. Sleeptite has everything—grace, style, and comfort.” I’m with Doris Day on this one.

WEDDING BELLE Dodie and Tad on the Day they were married.

During this mourning period, a few close friends have been visiting me for lunch and dinner, and I haven’t gone out. One day, the artist Jamian Juliano-Villani dropped by with Kat Herriman, a young writer friend of mine. Jamian said she likes her pajamas to be “versatile, so if you need to leave the house, you don’t look like a crazy person.” She wears two things on rotation—a Matouk robe and pajamas an art dealer gave her by the Copenhagen brand Tekla, which she wears outside. “They’re very, very cool. If you throw on a pair of sunglasses, you look great. They’re not cheap but they’re worth it.” She’s one of the few people I know who likes a matching set. “You feel more together. Go to bed, wake up….”

She does. I tell Jamian that I don’t know anybody who sleeps in their pajamas. Everyone I spoke to who wears them takes them off before going to bed—to sleep in the nude. (Not I.)

And not my friend Ruth Ganesh, who brought a herd of 100 life-size elephant sculptures made from the Lantana camara weed in Southern India to America to raise awareness for wildlife conservation. She wears Indian cotton pajamas, made in Jaipur using block technique. “They make the most beautiful multicolored ones, with flowers and patterns all over them, that give me the happiest dreams,” she tells me. “It’s a rite of passage when English people visitIndia to go pajama shopping in Anokhi. We stuff our suitcases full of them.”

Funny, Cecily Brown had told me that one of her dealers and a dear friend, Stefania Bortolami, gives her artist friends pajamas from Rome for Christmas. Seems pajamas-​as-​Christmas-​presents are a thing with art dealers and their artists. John Currin tells me that his London dealer, Sadie Coles, sends him ones from Turnbull & Asser for Christmas. The artist Diamond Stingily comes by with Pucci, her artist friend Martine Syms’s best-in-show Pomeranian, and my ears perk up when she tells me that the only place to get pajamas is a store called Schostal in Rome. “All the artists go there,” she says. Turns out artists know about the place because of Gavin Brown, whose Roman gallery is in Sant’Andrea de Scaphis, a ninth-​century deconsecrated church. Gavin and his wife, artist Hope Atherton, have introduced legions to the brand. Schostal pajamas are made of the finest materials, sewn with a sky-high thread count that makes them as soft as a baby mole’s skin and slightly see-through. They come in solids and stripes in mouthwatering colors.

I have to have a pair. However, I’m hopeless when it comes to ordering anything online, even FreshDirect. Then, Hope herself drops by for afternoon tea one Monday in June—and before I know it, a delicious pair of lemon Schostals with red-and-white pinstripes are winging their way to me from Rome. They’re not cheap—nearly $300—thanks to Trump’s tariffs.

The whole idea of wearing pajamas is to trick myself into feeling better. When I tell my friend and favorite dermatologist Joel Kassimir that I’ve decided to live in pajamas from now on, he says, “Like Peter Marino’s leathers, Julian Schnabel’s pajamas, and Vinny ‘Chin’ Gigante’s bathrobe, it is a uniform, and it works.”

The artist Rachel Feinstein brings me the best sashimi lunch from Sugarfish by Sushi Nozawa and we talk pajamas. She loves hers. “They’re by Dôen, a company that Flora (my 17-year-old daughter) is into, and she’s gotten me into them. It’s not really my style. They’re very Laura Ashley, actually—new Gen Z Laura Ashley. Made out of incredibly thin fine cotton. But I love them. They have a blue delft-like pattern, and the minute I’m home, I put them on. I don’t like silk—too cloying and hot.” No silk for me either. Or satin: too 1930s starlet boudoir—Carole Lombard, Claudette Colbert, Lauren Bacall, or Katharine Hepburn in Bringing Up Baby.

I can’t possibly make a decision about pajamas without talking to Vogue’s head of fashion, Virginia Smith. She’s running to catch a flight to Los Angeles when I reach her by phone, just in time for her to tell me about For Restless Sleepers, Olivia von Halle, and what she calls “the classics”—Charvet, Brooks Brothers, and Ralph Lauren. She also tells me about Grace Coddington wearing Michael Kors blue pajamas to the 2015 Met Gala—and that she herself wore Erdem mint pj’s to the 2024 Met Gala, “Sleeping Beauties.”

Last night I saw a woman on Park Avenue in matching pajamas walking her dog.

A few very close artist friends of Tad’s and mine have been keeping me afloat—or vertical, to use Tad’s word—throughout these difficult days, weeks, months without him. In the last 5 or 10 years of Tad’s life, whenever anyone asked him how he was doing, his answer was “I’m still vertical.”

Pajamas make me feel safe—and vertical—even though you wear them in a horizontal position. Pajamas are my safety net.

One mid-June sunny evening, Maurizio Cattelan and Anna Weyant come for dinner. Over the 30 years Tad and I have known Maurizio, every time he’d come for dinner, he’d surprise us with a wildly original present, each one topping the one before in outrageousness: ​a blowfish ceiling lamp; a human-size package of Oscar Mayer wieners; a Gucci box—open the cover and out pops a two-dimensional cutout of Tad and me. This time, he brings the tennis ball Billie Jean King signed for him the day before—he did a photo shoot with her for his magazine Toiletpaper. He mumbles something about the shoot and why she signed the tennis ball, but I don’t get it.

In advance of my birthday, which is the next day, Anna Weyant brings a present too—but hers is in a traditional white box tied up with a very pretty exaggeratedly wide vanilla grosgrain ribbon. It looks just like one of her hyperrealistic paintings. Inside is the perfect gift for me—the navy blue with white trim Eberjeys I’ve been dreaming about. “You can return them if you don’t like them,” she says. “No, I don’t want to return these,” I say with delight. I’m in pajama heaven.

“Will you wear sleepers?” Maurizio asks me.

After he repeats the word three times—“sleepers, sleepers, sleepers”—I finally get it. Slippers to go with my Eberjeys.

June 17: It’s my birthday, and I’m happily (and stylishly) wearing my new Eberjeys. They fit just right, make me feel safe, at home, sleek, well-dressed. These are going-out-in-the-world pajamas. They’re not 100 percent cotton but rather 95 percent Tencel Modal, a proud member of the rayon family, descended from the noble beech tree. Tencel promises all the benefits of cotton—super soft, durable, and a friend of the environment.

At three o’clock in the afternoon, Cecily Brown, Rachel Feinstein, Anna Weyant, and Kat Herriman surprise me with a pajama party. One by one they arrive and immediately change into their pj’s. Rachel didn’t have time to go home to get hers, but Cecily happens to have an extra pair in her bag—a fetching solid peach with navy trim. Rachel wears the top and bottom. She looks perfect, but nobody else dares.

The conversation roams all over the place, from what Cecily did the night she turned 30 to a book about witches and witchcraft called Abject Eroticism in Northern Renaissance Art.

I go to the Mark Hotel for dinner with my friend Peter Gelb, general manager of the Metropolitan Opera, in my navy blue Eberjeys with pearls. All I need are open-toe little satin bedroom slippers to complete my outfit. Nobody notices I’m wearing pajamas, not even Peter. But I know, and I know how much I need them. I need them forever. Or at least for now.

#6681. 25 Great Gifts for New Dads, According to GQ

Becoming a dad changes a lot of things. Your sleep schedule, for one. Your relationship with a clean shirt, for another. But just because a guy has entered his daddy era doesn't mean he's stopped caring about the things he cared about before.

With that in mind, we've rounded up the best gifts for new dads, with a little something for him and the little one. Some are practical things that'll make those early days of fatherhood a little easier. Others are simply things that'll make him feel good, look good, and a little more like himself.

Nothing doing? Check out the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

At some point, he'll emerge back into the world, and there's nothing like a great shirt to ease the reentry. This swaggy checked shirt from Beams has all the layering built right in, so he can look like he hasn't missed a step.

There's a lot to be said for clothes that don't require much thought, especially when you've got a new bundle. Take this double-faced merino wool bomber from Quince: warm, unfussy, and easy to throw on with just about anything.

Some brands really are thinking of the children. Everybody.World makes its Trash Zip Hoodie from 100% recycled cotton waste, giving discarded material a second life as a very good sweatshirt.

A good pair of sweatpants is nonnegotiable. From the true masters of the category, these midweight terry sweatpants from Reigning Champ come with a relaxed silhouette, an open hem, and a nicely lived-in patina.

The undisputed king of dad shoes has entered its seventh generation, with its first major redesign since 2022 bringing a sleeker suede-and-mesh upper, softer cushioning, and all the Made in USA pedigree you'd expect. For a guy who's just become a dad, the timing couldn't be better.

He's a dad now. A man of refinement, responsibility, and a pressing need for a do-it-all boot. Enter Blundstone's new Heritage boot, a top-shelf take on its legendary shit-stomper, upgraded with premium leather and Goodyear-welted construction.

The baby's developing a sense of sight, and there's no reason for dad to sacrifice his. Lalo's Play Gym II is a far better-looking alternative to what's out there, with plenty to keep little hands and eyes occupied, including sensory toys, teethers, and a bell. The brand's set of high-contrast art cards wouldn't hurt, either.

If they've already got a Tripp Trapp, this one's a no-brainer. The iconic high chair is part of MoMA's permanent collection, and now the museum's Design Store has a set of colorful cushions to go with it.

One thing new parents can never have enough of is a good place to put the baby down. Part quilt, part playmat, these organic cotton numbers from House of Noa are among the most handsome we've seen, with an heirloom quality that makes 'em worth holding on to long after the baby has outgrown tummy time.

The problem with BabyBjörn? Too many good things to choose from. But for new parents, the gift of a few hands-free minutes is hard to beat. The new Bouncer Begin is designed specifically for newborns, with a shallower seat than the brand's wildly popular Bouncer Bliss.

Bottle-washing is a dad duty. We don't make the rules. Baby Brezza's Bottle Washer Pro 360 makes the job considerably less miserable, washing, sterilizing, and drying bottles in one go.

Two things you can never have enough of with a newborn: muslin and blankets. Coyuchi's wonderfully soft muslin quilt takes care of both.

New dads live by the clock. Three hours between feeds, 20 minutes until the next nap, two minutes to themselves, if they're lucky. Braun's Time Teacher, with its clean, easy-to-read dial, colorful hands, and markings for phrases like "quarter past" and "half past," makes keeping track a little easier. And when the little one is old enough to tell time, it'll come in handy all over again.

Apple's finally getting into the smart display game. The new HomeView is the company's first dedicated smart home hub, bringing home controls, FaceTime, and the usual Apple ecosystem conveniences to one ittle screen. Its 12-megapixel camera should come in especially handy for keeping the grandparents supplied with baby sightings.

A sleeping baby is a beautiful thing. Hatch's portable Go sound machine is a little godsend, with soothing sounds, a rechargeable battery, and a handy clip for attaching it to the stroller or car seat.

Bose's new sport-minded open earbuds let him enjoy his music or a podcast without tuning out what's happening around him—like, say, an actual human baby. And on the rare occasion he gets out for a run, they'll be just as useful for logging a few miles.

For the dad with his hands full (read: all dads), Ray-Ban's Meta Zena glasses pair a snazzy cat-eye silhouette with the ability to capture first steps, film stroller outings, or video-call the grandparents, all without reaching for his phone.

Tiny Vinyl's miniature record player and four-inch records are pure novelty, but there's something rather charming about a tiny turntable for a tiny human. Start building the little one's record collection now, and they'll have something to grow into.

Fujifilm's new Instax Pal 2 gives dad another way to document his little one, packing a digital camera into an adorable, palm-sized package. He can send shots straight to his phone, or pair it with an Instax printer for a few keepsakes the grandparents can stick on the fridge.

there's something to be said for having a few memories you can actually hold in your hands. This new 35mm point-and-shoot from Kodak lets him capture the little one on film, with actual prints to show for it.

Coterie diapers really do live up to the hype. And the brand's skincare lineup is pretty terrific, too. This set brings together full-size bottles of its hair and body wash, all-over moisturizer, and diaper and dry skin balm.

Dad's going to need all the help he can get in the sleep department. No surprise there. What might surprise him is how much magnesium can help, from supporting normal muscle and nerve function to regulating the body's stress response and potentially improving sleep quality.

The Fitbit Air might be the sleekest screen-free fitness tracker around, and at a price that makes it an easy sell. For the new dad who just wants to keep tabs on his sleep and daily steps without getting too deep into the fitness-data weeds, it's a straightforward proposition.

A little time for some om-ing is a fine idea for any new dad. Walden's meditation set gives him a dedicated place to find his center, and the accompanying mat doubles as a nice spot for the little one to stretch out.

#6680. The Truth About ‘Natural Flavors’ On Food Labels Might Surprise You

The word “natural” comes with a few caveats.

I consider myself a pretty diligent ingredient-label reader. But there’s one phrase I see constantly that, until recently, I hadn’t given much thought to: “natural flavors.”

It’s printed on everything from flavored drinks to packaged snacks, and it sounds pretty straightforward. You’d probably assume that if something contains natural flavors, those flavors come directly from the foods they’re supposed to taste like. After all, that’s what natural suggests—except the actual definition is much broader than you might expect.

According to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), natural flavors can come from a surprisingly long list of sources, including fruits, vegetables, spices, herbs, dairy products, meat, seafood, and even certain fermentation products. And while those ingredients must come from qualifying sources, turning them into flavorings can be far more involved than simply squeezing juice from a fruit.

So what exactly does “natural flavors” mean, and how much does that label actually tell us about what’s in our food? Here’s what you should know.

The FDA’s definition of natural flavors focuses on where the flavoring comes from, not necessarily the food it’s supposed to taste like. Under federal regulations, natural flavors can include essential oils, extracts, distillates, and substances produced through roasting, heating, or enzymatic processing. They can originate from everything from fruit and vegetable juices to herbs, roots, bark, and fermentation products.

That means seeing “natural flavors” on a strawberry-flavored product doesn’t automatically mean the added flavoring came from strawberries.

Specific FDA rules govern how manufacturers describe flavors on the front of packages, particularly when a product’s recognizable flavor comes from sources other than the named food. But the generic ingredient-list declaration alone doesn’t identify the original source. In other words, the word “natural” doesn’t necessarily tell you what you’re tasting.

The FDA generally requires food manufacturers to list ingredients in descending order by weight. But flavorings are one category that can be declared collectively rather than listing every individual flavoring substance.

Under federal regulations, qualifying ingredients can simply appear as “natural flavor” or “natural flavors” on a product’s ingredient list. So manufacturers can use any combination of flavorings without disclosing the specific ones in your food.

There are exceptions, particularly for major food allergens, but the rule helps explain why the ingredient list doesn’t always provide a complete breakdown of a product’s flavor formulation.

The word “natural” tends to sound reassuring, especially when it’s printed on a product alongside claims about ingredients or quality. But it doesn’t automatically tell you anything about that food’s nutritional value.

According to the FDA, food ingredients must meet the same safety standard whether they’re naturally or artificially derived. The agency has also explained that its longstanding policy concerning the broader term “natural” on food labels was not intended to establish any particular nutritional or health benefit.

So while natural and artificial flavors differ in how they’re sourced, that distinction alone doesn’t establish that one is healthier, more nutritious, or safer than the other. And that feels like a pretty important distinction when you’re trying to make sense of the grocery aisle.

Another distinction worth knowing is that “natural” and “organic” don’t mean the same thing. The USDA has additional requirements for flavorings used in certified organic foods. Under federal organic regulations, manufacturers can use nonsynthetic flavors when organic flavors aren’t commercially available.

Those flavorings must come from organic or nonsynthetic sources and cannot be produced using synthetic solvents, synthetic carrier systems, or artificial preservatives. Those are additional restrictions beyond simply meeting the FDA’s definition of natural flavoring.

So while a conventional food and an organic food might both list natural flavors, that doesn’t necessarily mean the flavorings were produced under identical requirements.

The biggest takeaway is that natural flavors aren’t necessarily something to avoid. They’re just a lot less specific than many may assume. The label tells you that the flavoring meets the FDA’s definition of natural, but it doesn’t necessarily identify the ingredient it came from, explain how it was processed, or reveal every flavoring component. It also doesn’t automatically make the product healthier than something containing artificial flavors.

If you’re curious about what you’re eating, it helps to look beyond those two words. Check the full ingredient list, pay attention to how the product describes its flavor on the front of the package, and contact the manufacturer if you need more specific information about a flavoring’s source.

Ultimately, the most surprising thing about natural flavors is just how little those two words actually reveal.

#6679. Brittany Howard and Anna-Maria Babcock’s Tennessee Wedding Was a Celebration of Their Mexican and Southern Roots

Given their day jobs, musician Brittany Howard and record executive Anna-Maria Babcock’s meet-cute feels entirely appropriate: they first crossed paths at a concert. “We met at a friend’s album release show on October 10, 2023, at The Blue Room in Nashville,” Anna-Maria explains. Brittany, who is best known as the lead singer and guitarist of Alabama Shakes, was helping out at the merch table after the show. “I walked up to the table and a mutual friend introduced us by putting our hands in each other’s while asking, ‘Have y’all met yet?’ It was love at first sight for the both of us,” says Anna-Maria. A few days later, the two went on their first real date and fell in love over pizza rolls and mocktails at Brittany’s home. “The first date that never ended!” Anna-Maria jokes.

Just over a year later, Anna-Maria proposed on November 15, 2024, at Smith Lake in Alabama. After an extensive tour year, she encouraged Brittany to come with her on a fishing trip. “Little did I know, this was more than a fishing trip,” says Brittany. “On the first night of our stay, under the last full supermoon of the year, Anna-Maria got on one knee in a freshly made wood-fired hot tub. After the proposal, I said, ‘yes!’” Despite spending hours preparing the hot tub, the couple jumped out to share the news with their friends and family. “All those hours to prepare the hot tub, just to get out after five minutes! It’s okay though,” says Brittany. “We got all of our life together to make another fire.” Adds Anna-Maria, “Brittany followed up with a double proposal (the gay way) during our trip to Portugal for my birthday just a few months later! I also said yes to forever!”

Anna-Maria and Brittany spent the next two years planning their perfect wedding celebration. The big day arrived on October 24, 2026, at the Southall Farm & Inn in Franklin, Tennessee. The couple describes planning as both “so much fun” and “a lot of work.” “We had a hand in every single design aspect of the night; we wanted the space to feel like us,” says Anna-Maria. Alongside planner Carly Pickett, the brides lent their handwriting to save-the-dates, made an ofrenda to honor ancestors, and hand-selected planters from home to fill with florals. Says Anna-Maria, “We wanted our people to feel like they knew exactly whose wedding they were at—one that was very Black, very Mexican, and very queer!”

The couple also wanted to feel their cultures reflected through their fashion choices for the wedding weekend. “We wanted to feel gender affirmed, beautiful, sexy, and ourselves,” says Anna-Maria. “We were not interested in traditional wedding wear, so designing our own garments and sourcing from small women-owned, Black-owned, Indigenous-owned, and queer-owned brands was extremely important to us.” She adds that wearing family heirlooms was also an important part of their wardrobe curation. “We wanted our ancestors to be honored in this space,” says Anna-Maria.

For her wedding look, Brittany worked with stylist Courtney Mays to craft a custom gown with a detailed bodice and dramatic off-the-shoulder cape. Later in the evening, she changed into a bright red ensemble with diaphanous flowing fabric designed alongside Loulette Bride. Anna-Maria found a halter Danielle Frankel dress at Nashville bridal salon The Dress Theory. To walk down the aisle, she paired it with a veil from queer-owned brand Tanner Fletcher.

When Brittany changed into her red reception look, Anna-Maria changed into a textured, red dress of her own that was designed alongside Mays. The brides also created a mood board for their wedding party and even helped style some looks for them. “We wanted our wedding party to be more concerned with having fun, letting loose, and connecting with others—not with whether or not they liked the outfits we picked out for them that they will never wear again,” says Anna-Maria.

The weekend kicked off with an intimate sunset dinner overlooking the Tennessee hills. The rehearsal dinner was hosted by Anna-Maria’s parents, Sylvia and Randy Babcock. “We ate delicious Mexican food, danced to cumbia, and cried hysterically as our wedding party, parents, and grandmas expressed their love for us,” recalls Anna-Maria. “The feeling of watching your blood family and chosen family fall in love with each other was nothing short of magical and healing.”

The ceremony took place the next day in a meadow along a creek. Guests were surrounded by nature and gathered amongst florals that lined the aisle. “We walked to everyone’s smiling, expectant faces under a beautiful fall sunset while the mariachi band played a rendition of ‘The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face,’” describes Brittany. The couple walked towards one another on the arms of their parents. “When we got to the altar, we then encouraged our two-year-old nephew, who was the ring bearer, to come meet us up there! Holding a wooden fish ring box—the one Anna-Maria gifted me when she proposed—in one hand and picking his nose with the other, he joyfully ran up to us while stopping to smell the flowers halfway down the aisle,” she recalls. “A perfect reminder of what’s important in life. Always stop to smell the flowers.”

Anna-Maria’s Tía Pinky read a poem written by the bride’s late grandfather, Roberto. “His words reminded us of why we are here and why it’s important to not waste time with the ones we love,” says Brittany. Remembers Anna-Maria, “I was so giddy and my cheeks hurt from smiling so much. I felt so excited and humbled watching our family grow right before my eyes. I felt proud of myself for never giving up on love. Little us would be so proud.” Brittany emphasizes that she felt “full of pride” throughout the ceremony and as if the moment was “magical and sacred.” This magic was made complete as a rainbow appeared in the sky once the brides kissed. “We think that was a little sign from the ancestors that we were all right where we were supposed to be,” says Anna-Maria.

The mariachi band led the way towards the reception, followed by the newlyweds and their community as “Isn’t She Lovely” played. “We danced and sang our way around the lake to cocktail hour where the sun finally went down over the hill in a blaze of pinks, reds, purples and oranges,” recalls Brittany. “The moon was so bright it would stop us in our tracks.” Cocktail hour followed with reunions, hugs, and tears of joy. “We drank and danced to cumbia before walking over to the ofrenda to pay our respects to our loved ones who couldn’t physically be there with us,” says Anna-Maria. “We could feel their spirit throughout the entire night.”

The reception moved indoors for a dinner full of Mexican and Southern cuisine, along with a night full of music. “Lloyd Buchanan, who plays with my touring bands, led an incredible band during reception where he played our first dance song, ‘The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face’ by Roberta Flack in a hauntingly beautiful rendition,” says Brittany. “This song also happens to be Anna-Maria’s grandparents Maria and Roberto’s wedding song. Anna-Maria and I both took turns dancing to the end of the song with her 86-year-old grandmother.” She recalls, “There wasn’t a dry eye in the room.” The newlyweds then danced with their fathers and also did a special dance with their moms to “I Say A Little Prayer” by Aretha Franklin before welcoming all their guests onto the floor.

Special performances went on throughout the evening. “I come from a long line of family drummers, and my Uncle Scott and little brother Robert graced the stage, playing drums to Sinatra’s ‘Fly Me To The Moon’ and Bobby Caldwell’s ‘What You Won’t Do For Love’ respectively,” says Anna-Maria. “The very first time I saw live music, it was at an underground jazz club in DC where my uncle would play with his big band. When Uncle Scott was up there playing at the reception, I was instantly transported back to that club when I was a little girl.”

The after-party was held at Dottie’s, a speakeasy on the grounds of the property. The couple’s friend, DJ T1BG, spun until 2 a.m. “The room was vibrant with belly laughs, dirty dancing, wigs, bologna sandwiches, hot dogs, and deep conversations around the fire pit,” says Anna-Maria. “Our feet were aching—with Brittany nursing my blisters at 4 a.m.—but our hearts were exploding with love.” Adds Brittany, “We were so moved seeing our family and friends from thousands of miles away dancing together and making their own relationships. It’s the very thing we wanted our wedding to embody: communion.”

While the brides share they are truly excited to settle into their married lives with each other and enjoy the simplicity and joy of being newlyweds, they also emphasize how grateful they are to share their love today: “Getting married in the South as Black and brown lesbians feels extra heavy in today’s political climate. We live in a country where we have a Supreme Court justice who wants to ban interracial marriage. We live in a state where LGBTQIA+ rights are under attack, and the local government is working with ICE to tear families apart. We aren’t going anywhere. This is our home and we are here to stay. We are here to dig in deeper—into love and into our beautifully diverse and queer community. We believe love always wins, and it certainly felt like that at our wedding. While we were the first gay couple to get married at this venue in Franklin, Tennessee, we certainly won’t be the last!”

We started the most perfect weekend with our rehearsal dinner at golden hour overlooking the rolling hills of central Tennessee. Nothing beats Mexican food, our favorite people, cumbia music, and lots of happy tears. —Anna-Maria

We loved working with our wedding planner Carly Pickett on all paper goods! Carly also happens to be a close friend and an incredible visual artist, so working on these designs with her was so fun! We came up with our own custom gay quail lovers logo and custom icons to represent us as a couple. A lot of love went into these so that hopefully our guests could frame and display them in their homes to forever remember the special weekend we shared together. —Anna-Maria

My mom, dad, tías, and sister planned and decorated our beautiful rehearsal dinner. My mom has always been the party planner of the family—always making everyone feel so special and celebrated. The smells of the tortillas cooking, the floral arrangements made by my mom and sister Caroline, and the way the custom-made “Anna-Maria & Brittany” papel picado looked blowing in the breeze made us feel right at home. —Anna-Maria

#6678. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6677. Hailey! Demi! Keke! An Exclusive Behind-the-Scenes Look at the 2026 CFDA Awards

The biggest and brightest names in American fashion all came together last night for the 45th annual CFDA Awards, which are often referred to as the Oscars of Fashion. Taking place at New York’s Natural History Museum, the night celebrates both the unique contributions of American designers throughout the previous year and honors those who have made an indelible mark on the industry throughout their illustrious careers.

“Continue to share important stories and do work that means so much to you,” said CFDA chairman Thom Browne at the ceremony. “Work that you couldn’t imagine doing anything else, because the true marker of success is being able to do something you love always at the highest level. And never sacrifice the true creativity and quality of what you do.”

Awards were presented to Ralph Lauren, Rachel Scott of Diotima, the jewelry designer Ana Khouri, and Colleen Allen. Fashion world luminaries were also honored, including Tory Burch, Linda Fargo, Peter Marino, Susan Cianciolo, and Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin.

The night welcomed a retinue of A-listers to help celebrate, proving that fashion now touches every part of culture, from entertainment to tech to sports. Bold-faced names included the night’s host, Keke Palmer; presenters Zoe Kravitz, Hailey Bieber, Rosé, Lupita Nyong’o, Matt Damon, Naomi Osaka, Demi Moore, and Cole Escola; and celebrity attendees Gracie Abrams, Megan Thee Stallion, Travis Scott, PinkPantheress, and many more.

“Anthony is not only an extraordinary designer, but also an extraordinary human being,” said Zoe Kravitz while presenting Anthony Vaccarello with his honor for International Designer of the Year. “He has this rare ability to make you feel completely understood, and that is reflected in everything he creates.”

“Anthony doesn't just design clothes,” added Rosé. “He creates an attitude, a sense of freedom and confidence that is distinctly his own.”

Donatella Versace, who attended with Vaccarello, had this to say about the honor. “I love what Anthony has built at Saint Laurent over the last decade and cannot wait to see what he does next. New chapters are always inspiring.”

From the red carpet to the seated dinner to the ceremony and even behind-the-scenes, there were buzzy, celeb-filled such as this. To capture all the glitz and glamour, we sent photographer Hunter Abrams to bring you an exclusive look at all the action. Take a look below.

#6675. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6673. Inside Sophie Bille Brahe’s Danish Seaside Home, Where Every Object Tells a Story

It’s almost dusk in Copenhagen when jewelry designer Sophie Bille Brahe tells me over the phone that she’s about to take a quick dip in the ocean before dinner. It’s a small ritual tied to the reason she chose her five-bedroom, three-bathroom seaside home, 20 minutes north of the city center, in the first place. Designed by Danish architect Ib Lunding in 1929, the house sits on one of three small streets of similar homes in what Danes call the “flower neighborhood,” each one a slight variation on the next. For Bille Brahe, it’s this setting—and the sensory elements that come with it—that were non-negotiable. “I open up my window and I can see trees. I can smell the sea,” she says. “For me, that’s very important to have in my life every day.”

The space is a respite for the designer, who views the home as a collection of memories and a backdrop for her bustling family life, kids, and border collie included. It’s also where her namesake fine jewelry line begins. In fact, Bille Brahe often develops her designs within the home’s walls before she ever takes them to the workshop. “I sometimes catch these sensations, these small ideas, and make them a little bit more stable by doing drawings of them here at home. And then, when I have an idea of what I want to do, I’m ready to go to the workshop and start,” she explains. In those beginning stages, she works alone. “I need to be able to make really ugly things or really great things,” she says. “I need a bubble around me.”

That bubble is her workspace, an all-white room anchored by an 1870s Swedish fireplace Bille Brahe had installed when she moved in. “It has gold detailing, and it’s so beautiful,” she says. “A fireplace has a way of gathering family and speaks to a house built with love.” Nearby sits her desk, which belonged to her father’s best friend. “It’s basically where everything I make starts,” she says. “I’d loved it since I was a kid.”

Pulled up to the desk is a chair that visitors to her New York showroom may recognize: a curved stainless-steel design by Mats Theselius reupholstered in Sahco zebra fabric. The same seating appears in the showroom, a throughline between her personal and professional worlds. Marc Chagall’s Soleil Couchant, a Le Klint lamp, a neon work by Gun Gordillo, and a collection of seashells share the desk with her sketches and notes. The room opens onto the dining room, centered on a Børge Mogensen Øresund table surrounded by Gio Ponti chairs and a bouquet of sunflowers resting on it.

Of course, Bille Brahe furnished her boutiques with intention. In Copenhagen, she sought out one-of-a-kind Danish furniture and even began making her own vases in Murano. In New York, she tracked down a rare Poul Kjærholm table, square with a gray leather top instead of the round marble version many Danes grew up eating breakfast at. At home, she followed a similar rule and took her time, layering pieces slowly and making sure each one felt collected and had a story connected. “It took me many years to find a sofa, because every time I bought one I’d almost have a panic attack about the idea of buying something new, something everybody could have,” she says. “Everything I have in my home I’ve inherited, borrowed, or a friend made for me. If something doesn’t have a story, it doesn’t belong.”

Her jewel-toned Svenskt Tenn sofa is piled with pillows, each one a gift from a Swedish friend who came to visit. Beside it sits a slim side table, part drink trolley, stacked with books, a seashell, and a lamp she inherited from her grandfather. Most of the lighting in the house is inherited, except the Noguchi lanterns, which she brings back one at a time from trips to Japan. Another Japan find, the Nextmaruni Armless Chair by the architect duo SANAA (known as the Rabbit Chair for its ear-like back), sits beneath a pink painting by Danish artist Tal R.

Above all, though, it is a family house at its core. “It never feels like it’s an empty house,” she says. “I absolutely love my life with kids.” That’s particularly evident in the kitchen, where the day begins with coffee, breakfast for the kids, and, when the weather allows, the garden door thrown open. “It’s not a big house, so the kitchen needs to be efficient,” she says. “I cook a lot, so it ends up being a kitchen that can manage a lot of food without a lot of space.” Despite its small footprint, the room is warm, with kids’ art hung above the seating, embroidered tablecloths dressing the table, and an airy pendant overhead.

The same energy carries into the hallway, with its rounded window (a signature of the neighborhood’s houses) and walls in a blush pink by Farrow & Ball, the same color as the hallway in her previous home. When she moved, she changed everything else but kept the pink. “I normally don’t like colors on walls,” she says. “But I felt this was bringing something I used to love into the new house.”

Outside on the terrace, that pull toward nature continues. Every plant on the deck is one she’s had for 15 years or more, from a pomegranate tree she’s carried from home to home to the pink nerines called the “autumn flower,” and she has a story for each of them. According to Bille Brahe, there’s no need for more than this. If the trees are close enough to smell and the sea near enough to hear, she’s set and then some. “I’m not a person who needs a lot. I just need something close and clear, and if I have that, I can do what I need to do.”

#6672. Vietnamese Coffee Martini

You get dessert and a cocktail all in one with this Vietnamese coffee martini, which adds sweetened condensed milk to the classic espresso martini for a rich, frothy sip.

Whipping up a Vietnamese coffee martini after dinner means two things: You don’t have to make dessert, and you aren’t going to sleep anytime soon. This cocktail is next-level sweet and caffeinated, and it makes your regular espresso martini look like child’s play. Sure, this cocktail shares some of the same elements (vodka, coffee liqueur and espresso), but it includes sweetened condensed milk for a rich, luxurious texture, signature caramel sweetness and super-frothy finish.

Vietnamese coffee is typically made with dark-roasted robusta beans, which taste bolder and more chocolatey than the arabica beans in most coffee blends. In traditional preparations, the grounds drip slowly through a small metal filter called a phin, straight into a glass with a layer of sweetened condensed milk waiting at the bottom. Fresh milk was hard to come by and didn’t keep well in Vietnam’s heat, so canned milk became the go-to. It’s almost as thick as syrup and tastes a little like melted caramel. Shaken into a cocktail, it lands somewhere closer to a creamy Baileys espresso martini than a classic one, only richer.

Fill a cocktail shaker three-fourths full with ice. Add the vodka, espresso, sweetened condensed milk and Kahlua. Cover the shaker and shake hard until condensation forms on the outside, 10 to 15 seconds.

Strain the cocktail into a glass and top with the coffee beans. Serve immediately, while the foam is at its fluffiest.

Editor’s Tip: Chill your martini glass or coupe for 10 to 15 minutes before you start mixing. A frosty glass keeps the cocktail colder longer and helps the foam hold its shape.

Enjoy a Vietnamese coffee espresso martini right after you shake it, since the foam starts to deflate as it sits. If you’ve mixed up a little extra, store the unshaken mixture of vodka, coffee, condensed milk and Kahlua in a sealed jar in the refrigerator for up to two days. Give it a good stir, then shake it over fresh ice right before serving to revive the froth.

Making Vietnamese coffee martinis ahead of time is a smart move for hosting. Brew and chill the espresso or cold brew up to a day ahead, then mix the cocktail without ice. Refrigerate the batched cocktail until guests arrive. When it’s go time, shake each drink to order with fresh ice so every glass gets that signature foamy top.

For a dairy-free Vietnamese coffee martini, swap the regular sweetened condensed milk for sweetened condensed coconut milk. You should be able to find it in most grocery stores near the baking aisle. It shakes up just as creamy and sweet, with a subtle toasted coconut flavor that plays beautifully with the coffee. Kahlua is dairy-free, so the rest of the recipe stays the same.

Vietnamese coffee is usually made with robusta beans, which have nearly twice the caffeine of the arabica beans used in most espresso blends. Ounce for ounce, phin-brewed Vietnamese coffee can rival a shot of espresso, which is why it stands up so well to sweet condensed milk.

The foam comes from the oils in freshly brewed coffee, so espresso gives you the most dramatic froth, while cold brew and instant coffee create a slightly thinner layer. The condensed milk helps, too, adding body that traps air bubbles as you shake. Use plenty of ice, shake like you mean it and strain right away into a chilled glass so the foam settles on top in a smooth, creamy cap.

#6671. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6670. The Halloween Candy That Matches Your Zodiac Sign, According To An Astrologer

Whether you fully commit to spooky season or prefer to keep things low-key, you can’t truly celebrate Halloween without enjoying some candy. Different sweets have cultivated fierce brand loyalties. But the key to finding your favorite Halloween candy may be hiding among the stars.

We consulted astrologer and author Lisa Stardust to find which candy best reflects each zodiac sign's personality. From old-school chocolates to wild, wacky treats, her choices span the full sweet spectrum.

Aries is defined by its bold and ambitious approach to life. Stardust describes the cardinal fire sign as “passionate, electrifying, and intense.” But Aries can also be a bit impulsive. “You never know what you’re going to get next based on their emotions,” she adds.

In honor of Aries’ fiery spirit, Stardust chooses Hot Tamales as the candy that best reflects the sign. With its vibrant red hue, intense spice, and unapologetic cinnamon-forward flavor, there’s no better sweet to symbolize the sign.

Compared to Aries' bold energy, Taurus is decidedly more practical. The earth sign is known for being stable, dependable, and guided by logic over emotion. While Taurus may resist change, the sign also has good taste and knows its way around the finer things in life.

And what candy represents that tried-and-true energy better than a classic bar of Hershey’s milk chocolate? “They’re both iconic and never go out of style,” Stardust explains. “Their tastes might be simple, but they’re always decadent and indulgent.”

Gemini is the astrological embodiment of street smarts. The air sign is very astute, with the uncanny ability to read a room and adapt accordingly. This perceptiveness translates to strong social skills and the ability to elevate the mood of any room.

The candy that best reflects this energy is, unsurprisingly, Smarties. “Geminis are intellectual, and they have a little bit of zest to them,” explains Stardust. “They’re sugary and sweet but also a little messy.”

The cardinal water sign is not shy about expressing emotions. Cancers are best described as the teddy bears of the zodiac: sensitive, empathetic, and the embodiment of comfort. Those with Cancer in their chart are prone to shielding others from their complex emotions, but make no mistake—there are a lot of feelings.

A candy that matches Cancer’s mushy inner self is Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups. “They are very protective on the outside, but they're tender on the inside,” Stardust says.

Leo can’t help but be the life of the party. The fire sign is very extroverted, with a personality so big it verges on theatrical. Stardust describes Leos as “fun and flamboyant,” even if they sometimes get on other people’s nerves.

In her opinion, the sweets that represent Leo best are Twizzlers. Stardust notes that you “can have a lot of fun eating them,” whether it’s peeling them apart or biting off the ends to use as a straw. If it involves playing with your food, it’s perfect for Leo.

Virgos are Type A to their cores. The earth sign has a precise attention to detail and is always looking to solve problems. But the constant focus on logic and perfection often obscures a deep well of emotions.

“There’s more to them than you may think, and there’s definitely another flavor to them on the inside, because they’re ruled by Mercury,” Stardust explains. The candy that best mirrors this energy is a York Peppermint Patty. The seemingly simple chocolate exterior hides a sweet, sharp minty center (if that’s not Virgo, I don’t know what is).

Libra is represented by scales, which reflects the air sign’s desire for fairness and justice. The empathetic and compassionate Libra tends to consider all points of view to make the most measured decisions that’ll make everyone happy. (But sometimes, that may mean not making a decision at all.)

Libra’s balanced approach to life is why Stardust chooses Twix as their ideal candy. Left Twix or right Twix? Thankfully, Libra doesn’t have to choose. “They’re a package deal,” Stardust says. So whether they want to enjoy both or share with someone else, Libras are Twix’s target audience.

Scorpios embody the phrase, “looks like they could kill you, is a cinnamon roll.” The water sign is often misunderstood. While undoubtedly intense, Scorpio’s dark, almost brooding exterior hides a lot of emotional complexity.

The sign shares a lot of characteristics with one candy in particular: Sour Patch Kids. “They have a really deep personality to them; they’re sweet with a sharp, tangy bite.” And, like the multicolored gummy treats, Scorpio is the true manifestation of “sour, sweet, gone.”

Sagittarius is seemingly always on a journey—whether it be physical, emotional, or spiritual. The fire sign is known as an explorer, with lofty aspirations and an aversion to playing it safe.

This energy is exactly why Stardust chooses 3 Musketeers as the quintessential Sagittarius sweet. “The namesake is adventurous, and it speaks for itself,” she explains.

When you need someone reliable, responsible, and grounded, you can’t go wrong with a Capricorn. This pragmatic, logical earth sign is incredibly goal-oriented and has the Type A personality to make it happen.

How many licks does it take to get to the center of a Tootsie Pop? Capricorn may be the only sign in the zodiac that’s disciplined enough to find out, which is why Stardust chooses the lollipop as their ideal candy. “It’s a classic, just like Capricorn,” she says. “They’re traditional, steady, strong, and you have to have patience to eat them.”

Aquarius marches to the beat of its own drummer. The air sign loves to be a contrarian and will unapologetically take the road less traveled. Nothing is too unique or too strange for Aquarius.

And what candy matches that energy better than a bag of Pop Rocks? “They’re unexpected and veer from the norm of traditional candy,” Stardust explains. They’re shocking, surprising, and delightful in their own special way—just like Aquarius loves to be.

Pisces always seems to have its head in the clouds. The water sign has a dreamy, romantic approach to life and has an extremely vivid imagination. “They feel all the feels,” Stardust explains.

Pisces needs a candy that can keep up mentally and emotionally, which is why she chooses Skittles as their ideal sweet. “It’s all about the rainbow and the imagination,” Stardust says. “They get to taste the rainbow and all of the sensations in every bite.”
